Evidence (what the judge was shown; for an image, a description of what was sent)
You have four datasets worth applying to. UK Biobank is the best fit. NHANES is the quickest to start with. Whitehall II is a smaller wrist-based option with hospital-record linkage. All of Us is the only one that comes with caveats about wrist placement. I checked each by search. The UK Biobank and NSRR (National Sleep Research Resource) pages themselves wouldn't load for me, so some details come from secondary sources, and I flag those below.

## Main candidates

**1. UK Biobank** (wrist, about 100,000 people, hospital and death linkage)
- **Device:** Axivity AX3 worn on the dominant wrist for 7 days at 100 Hz. About 103,700 participants returned data between 2013 and 2015. The raw data are field 90001, and the wear-time and calibration QC fields are listed in the official accelerometer documentation. ([Doherty 2017](https://biobank.ndph.ox.ac.uk/showcase/ukb/docs/acc_plos_0169649.pdf), [UKB protocol PDF](https://biobank.ndph.ox.ac.uk/ukb/ukb/docs/PhysicalActivityMonitor.pdf))
- **Outcomes:** Published work uses it for incident disease and mortality ([npj Digital Medicine](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-022-00676-9)). I didn't separately confirm the hospital and death linkage details, but this is how it is normally used.
- **Access:**
  - Register, then submit an application. Your institution must sign a contract (a Material Transfer Agreement), and international applicants are accepted. Once approved, you have 90 days to pay and sign.
  - Data are accessed only through the cloud Research Analysis Platform. Compute is billed separately, with a small starting credit.
  - Reported fees are £3,000 for Tier 1 and £9,000 for Tier 3 (3 years), excluding VAT, payable in GBP. Students anywhere can get access for £500. ([Fees](https://www.ukbiobank.ac.uk/use-our-data/fees/), [FAQ](https://community.ukbiobank.ac.uk/hc/en-gb/articles/28002689502237-Applying-to-UK-Biobank-and-accessing-data-FAQ))
  - UK Biobank's FAQ gives an average of about 15 weeks from submission to data release.
- **Check first:** One secondary source says new applications were paused in mid-2026 during a platform upgrade. I couldn't confirm this on UK Biobank's own pages, so verify before you plan around it.

**2. NHANES 2011–2014** (wrist, US-representative, mortality only)
- **Device:** ActiGraph GT3X+ worn on the wrist for up to 9 days, for ages 6 and up, released in 2020. The data are in MIMS units, so comparability with other brands depends on harmonization.
- **Outcomes:** NCHS public-use linked mortality files give vital status, cause of death and follow-up through 31 Dec 2019. A published analysis of ages 50–80 had 3,653 participants and 416 deaths. ([MSSE paper](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11402588/), [NCHS linkage](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data-linkage/mortality-public.htm))
- **Access:** Both datasets are free to download with no application. The public file covers death only, with no hospital records.

**3. Whitehall II accelerometer sub-study** (wrist, about 4,000 people, mortality and hospital linkage)
- **Device:** GENEActiv on the non-dominant wrist, 9 days, in 2012–13. About 4,000 participants had valid data.
- **Outcomes:** Linked to mortality (about 8 years of follow-up) and to Hospital Episode Statistics. It has also been used for cardiovascular disease incidence. ([Sci Rep 2025](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-30237-5))
- **Access:** By application through UCL's Whitehall II data-sharing page. It isn't public because of ethics restrictions. The UCL URLs have moved over time, so use the [current page](https://www.ucl.ac.uk/epidemiology-health-care/research/epidemiology-and-public-health/research/whitehall-ii/data-sharing). I didn't find the fee or timeline.
- **Why it's useful:** The cohort is small enough to replicate UK Biobank findings against.

## Use with caveats

**4. All of Us (Fitbit)**
- **Data:** About 59,000 participants with Fitbit data, linked to electronic health records. ([Nature Medicine 2026](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-026-04352-3))
- **Wrist placement:** I found no source documenting it, and device model isn't available in the Workbench. That undercuts your comparability goal. Treat it as consumer-tracker data, not research-grade wrist accelerometry.
- **Outcomes:** Death comes from health records and participant status reports, not a national death registry. In the Registered Tier the death dates are shifted and cause is suppressed. ([death data](https://support.researchallofus.org/hc/en-us/articles/10237876482196-How-to-find-participant-death-reports))
- **Access:** Your institution needs a signed Data Use and Registration Agreement. Individual researchers then register, complete ethics training and attest to the data use agreement. Analysis happens in the cloud Workbench, with no downloads. Recent Fitbit papers used the Controlled Tier. ([overview](https://casrai.org/guides/all-of-us-researcher-workbench-tiered-access))

**5. MrOS Sleep Study and Study of Osteoporotic Fractures (SOF)**
- **MrOS:** Older US men, about 3,000 with 3–5 days of wrist actigraphy (Sleepwatch-O), and published mortality analyses exist. ([Paudel](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20370475)) However, the NSRR page states that no actigraphy is included. The actigraphy has to be requested from the MrOS Sleep Study investigators. ([PLOS ONE](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0285703)) NSRR itself uses a request form with a data use agreement and IRB documentation. ([NSRR MrOS](https://sleepdata.org/datasets/mros))
- **SOF:** Older women with wrist actigraphy (at least three 24-hour periods) and mortality follow-up. NSRR lists it with a request button. ([circadian rhythm paper](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2938873/), [NSRR SOF](https://sleepdata.org/datasets/sof)) I didn't confirm the sample size or exactly what is released.
- **Limits:** Both are older-adult and single-sex samples, and the actigraphy is from the 2000s, so they are less comparable with modern wrist devices. MrOS's actigraph is single-axis.

## Not confirmed
- **Our Future Health:** My search found nothing on wearable data or access, so I can't recommend it.
- **Women's Health Initiative OPACH:** It used hip-worn ActiGraph devices, so it fails your wrist criterion.

## Suggested plan
Start with NHANES, which needs no application. Apply to UK Biobank in parallel and check its application status first. Whitehall II gives you a second wrist cohort with hospital linkage for replication. If you want, I can look into the Whitehall II and NSRR access steps next, or the NCHS restricted linkage through the Research Data Center, which would add non-fatal outcomes for NHANES. I haven't searched for that.

Evidence (what the judge was shown; for an image, a description of what was sent)
You have four datasets worth applying to. UK Biobank is the best fit. NHANES is the quickest to start with. Whitehall II is a smaller wrist-based option with hospital-record linkage. All of Us is the only one that comes with caveats about wrist placement. I checked each by search. The UK Biobank and NSRR (National Sleep Research Resource) pages themselves wouldn't load for me, so some details come from secondary sources, and I flag those below.

## Main candidates

**1. UK Biobank** (wrist, about 100,000 people, hospital and death linkage)
- **Device:** Axivity AX3 worn on the dominant wrist for 7 days at 100 Hz. About 103,700 participants returned data between 2013 and 2015. The raw data are field 90001, and the wear-time and calibration QC fields are listed in the official accelerometer documentation. ([Doherty 2017](https://biobank.ndph.ox.ac.uk/showcase/ukb/docs/acc_plos_0169649.pdf), [UKB protocol PDF](https://biobank.ndph.ox.ac.uk/ukb/ukb/docs/PhysicalActivityMonitor.pdf))
- **Outcomes:** Published work uses it for incident disease and mortality ([npj Digital Medicine](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-022-00676-9)). I didn't separately confirm the hospital and death linkage details, but this is how it is normally used.
- **Access:**
  - Register, then submit an application. Your institution must sign a contract (a Material Transfer Agreement), and international applicants are accepted. Once approved, you have 90 days to pay and sign.
  - Data are accessed only through the cloud Research Analysis Platform. Compute is billed separately, with a small starting credit.
  - Reported fees are £3,000 for Tier 1 and £9,000 for Tier 3 (3 years), excluding VAT, payable in GBP. Students anywhere can get access for £500. ([Fees](https://www.ukbiobank.ac.uk/use-our-data/fees/), [FAQ](https://community.ukbiobank.ac.uk/hc/en-gb/articles/28002689502237-Applying-to-UK-Biobank-and-accessing-data-FAQ))
  - UK Biobank's FAQ gives an average of about 15 weeks from submission to data release.
- **Check first:** One secondary source says new applications were paused in mid-2026 during a platform upgrade. I couldn't confirm this on UK Biobank's own pages, so verify before you plan around it.

**2. NHANES 2011–2014** (wrist, US-representative, mortality only)
- **Device:** ActiGraph GT3X+ worn on the wrist for up to 9 days, for ages 6 and up, released in 2020. The data are in MIMS units, so comparability with other brands depends on harmonization.
- **Outcomes:** NCHS public-use linked mortality files give vital status, cause of death and follow-up through 31 Dec 2019. A published analysis of ages 50–80 had 3,653 participants and 416 deaths. ([MSSE paper](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11402588/), [NCHS linkage](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data-linkage/mortality-public.htm))
- **Access:** Both datasets are free to download with no application. The public file covers death only, with no hospital records.

**3. Whitehall II accelerometer sub-study** (wrist, about 4,000 people, mortality and hospital linkage)
- **Device:** GENEActiv on the non-dominant wrist, 9 days, in 2012–13. About 4,000 participants had valid data.
- **Outcomes:** Linked to mortality (about 8 years of follow-up) and to Hospital Episode Statistics. It has also been used for cardiovascular disease incidence. ([Sci Rep 2025](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-30237-5))
- **Access:** By application through UCL's Whitehall II data-sharing page. It isn't public because of ethics restrictions. The UCL URLs have moved over time, so use the [current page](https://www.ucl.ac.uk/epidemiology-health-care/research/epidemiology-and-public-health/research/whitehall-ii/data-sharing). I didn't find the fee or timeline.
- **Why it's useful:** The cohort is small enough to replicate UK Biobank findings against.

## Use with caveats

**4. All of Us (Fitbit)**
- **Data:** About 59,000 participants with Fitbit data, linked to electronic health records. ([Nature Medicine 2026](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-026-04352-3))
- **Wrist placement:** I found no source documenting it, and device model isn't available in the Workbench. That undercuts your comparability goal. Treat it as consumer-tracker data, not research-grade wrist accelerometry.
- **Outcomes:** Death comes from health records and participant status reports, not a national death registry. In the Registered Tier the death dates are shifted and cause is suppressed. ([death data](https://support.researchallofus.org/hc/en-us/articles/10237876482196-How-to-find-participant-death-reports))
- **Access:** Your institution needs a signed Data Use and Registration Agreement. Individual researchers then register, complete ethics training and attest to the data use agreement. Analysis happens in the cloud Workbench, with no downloads. Recent Fitbit papers used the Controlled Tier. ([overview](https://casrai.org/guides/all-of-us-researcher-workbench-tiered-access))

**5. MrOS Sleep Study and Study of Osteoporotic Fractures (SOF)**
- **MrOS:** Older US men, about 3,000 with 3–5 days of wrist actigraphy (Sleepwatch-O), and published mortality analyses exist. ([Paudel](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20370475)) However, the NSRR page states that no actigraphy is included. The actigraphy has to be requested from the MrOS Sleep Study investigators. ([PLOS ONE](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0285703)) NSRR itself uses a request form with a data use agreement and IRB documentation. ([NSRR MrOS](https://sleepdata.org/datasets/mros))
- **SOF:** Older women with wrist actigraphy (at least three 24-hour periods) and mortality follow-up. NSRR lists it with a request button. ([circadian rhythm paper](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2938873/), [NSRR SOF](https://sleepdata.org/datasets/sof)) I didn't confirm the sample size or exactly what is released.
- **Limits:** Both are older-adult and single-sex samples, and the actigraphy is from the 2000s, so they are less comparable with modern wrist devices. MrOS's actigraph is single-axis.

## Not confirmed
- **Our Future Health:** My search found nothing on wearable data or access, so I can't recommend it.
- **Women's Health Initiative OPACH:** It used hip-worn ActiGraph devices, so it fails your wrist criterion.

## Suggested plan
Start with NHANES, which needs no application. Apply to UK Biobank in parallel and check its application status first. Whitehall II gives you a second wrist cohort with hospital linkage for replication. If you want, I can look into the Whitehall II and NSRR access steps next, or the NCHS restricted linkage through the Research Data Center, which would add non-fatal outcomes for NHANES. I haven't searched for that.

These are the datasets I'd consider, ordered by how well they fit your criteria. I checked each against web sources, and I flag below what I couldn't confirm.

## Primary candidates

### 1. UK Biobank (best fit for your design)
- **Wrist data:** About 103,700 participants wore an Axivity AX3 on the dominant wrist for 7 days at 100 Hz, in 2013–2015. Raw data is in field 90001, with quality-control fields for wear time and calibration.
- **Outcomes:** The cohort has linked hospital records and death registrations, and many published papers use the accelerometer subsample. I didn't open a page describing the linkage itself, so confirm the current follow-up dates in the Data Showcase.
- **Access:**
  - Register (free, reviewed in about 10 working days), then submit an application. Applications are approved for health-related research in the public interest, and your US university is fine.
  - After approval you have 90 days to pay the access fee and sign the Material Transfer Agreement (MTA). UK Biobank's FAQ gives an average of about 15 weeks from submission to data release.
  - The fee is cost-recovery. I found £500 + VAT for students (3 years of access). I couldn't find a current standard fee: the older £1,500 + VAT figure I saw is from 2020 and out of date. Check the current schedule.
  - Analysis takes place on the cloud Research Analysis Platform (run by DNAnexus), which has separate storage and compute charges. New users get £40 of credit.
- **Caveat:** The cohort is healthier and less diverse than the general population. This matters for generalisability but not for comparability with other wrist studies.

### 2. NHANES 2011–2014 (US, nationally representative)
- **Wrist data:** An ActiGraph GT3X+ was worn on the non-dominant wrist for 7 days at 80 Hz. About 12,600 participants across the two waves have accelerometer data, and the data were released in December 2020. Many of them are children, so you'd restrict to adults.
- **Outcomes:** Linkage is to the National Death Index, so you get mortality only, not hospital diagnoses. NCHS's public-use linked mortality files page says follow-up runs through 31 Dec 2022. A search summary said 2019, so check which version you're using.
- **Access:**
  - Accelerometer data and public-use mortality files are free downloads with no application. Minute-level derived data is also on PhysioNet.
  - Restricted-use mortality files (unaltered, including children) are available only through an NCHS Research Data Center with an approved project. You can't combine public-use and restricted-use files inside the RDC.
- **Caveat:** The device and wrist differ from UK Biobank (ActiGraph on the non-dominant wrist, versus Axivity on the dominant wrist). That is a comparability issue if you pool or replicate across the two.

### 3. All of Us (US, with linked EHR)
- **Wrist data:** Fitbit data covers participants who chose to share it. It comes as summary and minute-level tables derived from Fitbit's proprietary algorithms, and raw accelerometry is not provided. That limits comparability with raw-signal wrist studies like UK Biobank and NHANES.
- **Outcomes:** The linked EHR gives diagnoses. Registered Tier Fitbit data is date-shifted.
- **Access:**
  - Your institution must sign a Data Use and Registration Agreement (DURA).
  - You then register, verify your identity, complete Responsible Conduct of Research training, and attest to a code of conduct.
  - There is no project pre-approval, and the data access is free (you may pay for compute and storage).
  - A recent FAQ describes a move to a new Verily-based platform, so check the current onboarding.
- **Caveat:** I'd treat this as a supplementary or sensitivity dataset, because it uses consumer devices with proprietary metrics and has a self-selected wearer subsample. I didn't confirm sample size or Fitbit wear duration. Check the Nature Medicine wearables paper for those.

## Smaller wrist-actigraphy cohorts (older adults)
These are likely under "a few thousand" and have more restricted access, so I'd use them for replication.

- **Study of Osteoporotic Fractures (SOF):** About 3,676 women were eligible for wrist actigraphy at Exam 8 (2002–2003), and a published SOF analysis linked circadian rhythms to mortality. Sleep-visit data are on the National Sleep Research Resource (NSRR), which has a "Request Data Access" option. SOF data are also available through SOF Online and NIA's AgingResearchBiobank. I didn't verify whether the NSRR release includes the raw actigraphy or only summaries.
- **MrOS (men only, N≈2,600):** The Sleepwatch-O is a wrist actigraph. NSRR hosts the polysomnography data but not the actigraphy. Actigraphy requests go to the MrOS sleep study investigators (California Pacific Medical Center Research Institute) or the SOF/MrOS Coordinating Center.
- **Whitehall II (UK):** A paper used wrist accelerometry with mortality follow-up to October 2023. Access is through the UCL data sharing portal. A preprint says the data can't be shared publicly because of ethics constraints, so expect a controlled application. I didn't check the portal's requirements.

## What I couldn't verify
- I couldn't open UK Biobank's own application page (the site returned a 403), so the fee and timeline details come from its FAQ and search summaries.
- I found nothing on the Women's Health Study. The Women's Health Initiative OPACH study used hip-worn devices, so it doesn't meet your wrist requirement.

## Suggested approach
Use UK Biobank as your main analysis, since it is the largest dataset and has hospital and death linkage. Use NHANES for a free US replication, with the caveat that it covers mortality only and uses a different device and wrist. Add SOF or MrOS if you want an older-adult cohort and can wait for controlled access. I can look further into any one of these, such as UK Biobank's current fee schedule or the SOF/MrOS proposal process.

- [UK Biobank Physical Activity Monitor documentation](https://biobank.ndph.ox.ac.uk/ukb/ukb/docs/PhysicalActivityMonitor.pdf)
- [UK Biobank: Applying and accessing data FAQ](https://community.ukbiobank.ac.uk/hc/en-gb/articles/28002689502237-Applying-to-UK-Biobank-and-accessing-data-FAQ)

  - Register (free, reviewed in about 10 working days), then submit an application. Applications are approved for health-related research in the public interest, and your US university is fine.
  - After approval you have 90 days to pay the access fee and sign the Material Transfer Agreement (MTA). UK Biobank's FAQ gives an average of about 15 weeks from submission to data release.
  - The fee is cost-recovery. I found £500 + VAT for students (3 years of access). I couldn't find a current standard fee: the older £1,500 + VAT figure I saw is from 2020 and out of date. Check the current schedule.
  - Analysis takes place on the cloud Research Analysis Platform (run by DNAnexus), which has separate storage and compute charges. New users get £40 of credit.
- **Caveat:** The cohort is healthier and less diverse than the general population. This matters for generalisability but not for comparability with other wrist studies.

### 2. NHANES 2011–2014 (US, nationally representative)
- **Wrist data:** An ActiGraph GT3X+ was worn on the non-dominant wrist for 7 days at 80 Hz. About 12,600 participants across the two waves have accelerometer data, and the data were released in December 2020. Many of them are children, so you'd restrict to adults.
- **Outcomes:** Linkage is to the National Death Index, so you get mortality only, not hospital diagnoses. NCHS's public-use linked mortality files page says follow-up runs through 31 Dec 2022. A search summary said 2019, so check which version you're using.
- **Access:**
  - Accelerometer data and public-use mortality files are free downloads with no application. Minute-level derived data is also on PhysioNet.
  - Restricted-use mortality files (unaltered, including children) are available only through an NCHS Research Data Center with an approved project. You can't combine public-use and restricted-use files inside the RDC.
- **Caveat:** The device and wrist differ from UK Biobank (ActiGraph on the non-dominant wrist, versus Axivity on the dominant wrist). That is a comparability issue if you pool or replicate across the two.

### 3. All of Us (US, with linked EHR)
- **Wrist data:** Fitbit data covers participants who chose to share it. It comes as summary and minute-level tables derived from Fitbit's proprietary algorithms, and raw accelerometry is not provided. That limits comparability with raw-signal wrist studies like UK Biobank and NHANES.
- **Outcomes:** The linked EHR gives diagnoses. Registered Tier Fitbit data is date-shifted.
- **Access:**
  - Your institution must sign a Data Use and Registration Agreement (DURA).
  - You then register, verify your identity, complete Responsible Conduct of Research training, and attest to a code of conduct.
  - There is no project pre-approval, and the data access is free (you may pay for compute and storage).
  - A recent FAQ describes a move to a new Verily-based platform, so check the current onboarding.
- **Caveat:** I'd treat this as a supplementary or sensitivity dataset, because it uses consumer devices with proprietary metrics and has a self-selected wearer subsample. I didn't confirm sample size or Fitbit wear duration. Check the Nature Medicine wearables paper for those.

## Smaller wrist-actigraphy cohorts (older adults)
These are likely under "a few thousand" and have more restricted access, so I'd use them for replication.

- **Study of Osteoporotic Fractures (SOF):** About 3,676 women were eligible for wrist actigraphy at Exam 8 (2002–2003), and a published SOF analysis linked circadian rhythms to mortality. Sleep-visit data are on the National Sleep Research Resource (NSRR), which has a "Request Data Access" option. SOF data are also available through SOF Online and NIA's AgingResearchBiobank. I didn't verify whether the NSRR release includes the raw actigraphy or only summaries.
- **MrOS (men only, N≈2,600):** The Sleepwatch-O is a wrist actigraph. NSRR hosts the polysomnography data but not the actigraphy. Actigraphy requests go to the MrOS sleep study investigators (California Pacific Medical Center Research Institute) or the SOF/MrOS Coordinating Center.
- **Whitehall II (UK):** A paper used wrist accelerometry with mortality follow-up to October 2023. Access is through the UCL data sharing portal. A preprint says the data can't be shared publicly because of ethics constraints, so expect a controlled application. I didn't check the portal's requirements.

## What I couldn't verify
- I couldn't open UK Biobank's own application page (the site returned a 403), so the fee and timeline details come from its FAQ and search summaries.
- I found nothing on the Women's Health Study. The Women's Health Initiative OPACH study used hip-worn devices, so it doesn't meet your wrist requirement.

## Suggested approach
Use UK Biobank as your main analysis, since it is the largest dataset and has hospital and death linkage. Use NHANES for a free US replication, with the caveat that it covers mortality only and uses a different device and wrist. Add SOF or MrOS if you want an older-adult cohort and can wait for controlled access. I can look further into any one of these, such as UK Biobank's current fee schedule or the SOF/MrOS proposal process.

These are the datasets I'd consider, ordered by how well they fit your criteria. I checked each against web sources, and I flag below what I couldn't confirm.

## Primary candidates

### 1. UK Biobank (best fit for your design)
- **Wrist data:** About 103,700 participants wore an Axivity AX3 on the dominant wrist for 7 days at 100 Hz, in 2013–2015. Raw data is in field 90001, with quality-control fields for wear time and calibration.
- **Outcomes:** The cohort has linked hospital records and death registrations, and many published papers use the accelerometer subsample. I didn't open a page describing the linkage itself, so confirm the current follow-up dates in the Data Showcase.
- **Access:**
  - Register (free, reviewed in about 10 working days), then submit an application. Applications are approved for health-related research in the public interest, and your US university is fine.
  - After approval you have 90 days to pay the access fee and sign the Material Transfer Agreement (MTA). UK Biobank's FAQ gives an average of about 15 weeks from submission to data release.
  - The fee is cost-recovery. I found £500 + VAT for students (3 years of access). I couldn't find a current standard fee: the older £1,500 + VAT figure I saw is from 2020 and out of date. Check the current schedule.
  - Analysis takes place on the cloud Research Analysis Platform (run by DNAnexus), which has separate storage and compute charges. New users get £40 of credit.
- **Caveat:** The cohort is healthier and less diverse than the general population. This matters for generalisability but not for comparability with other wrist studies.

### 2. NHANES 2011–2014 (US, nationally representative)
- **Wrist data:** An ActiGraph GT3X+ was worn on the non-dominant wrist for 7 days at 80 Hz. About 12,600 participants across the two waves have accelerometer data, and the data were released in December 2020. Many of them are children, so you'd restrict to adults.
- **Outcomes:** Linkage is to the National Death Index, so you get mortality only, not hospital diagnoses. NCHS's public-use linked mortality files page says follow-up runs through 31 Dec 2022. A search summary said 2019, so check which version you're using.
- **Access:**
  - Accelerometer data and public-use mortality files are free downloads with no application. Minute-level derived data is also on PhysioNet.
  - Restricted-use mortality files (unaltered, including children) are available only through an NCHS Research Data Center with an approved project. You can't combine public-use and restricted-use files inside the RDC.
- **Caveat:** The device and wrist differ from UK Biobank (ActiGraph on the non-dominant wrist, versus Axivity on the dominant wrist). That is a comparability issue if you pool or replicate across the two.

### 3. All of Us (US, with linked EHR)
- **Wrist data:** Fitbit data covers participants who chose to share it. It comes as summary and minute-level tables derived from Fitbit's proprietary algorithms, and raw accelerometry is not provided. That limits comparability with raw-signal wrist studies like UK Biobank and NHANES.
- **Outcomes:** The linked EHR gives diagnoses. Registered Tier Fitbit data is date-shifted.
- **Access:**
  - Your institution must sign a Data Use and Registration Agreement (DURA).
  - You then register, verify your identity, complete Responsible Conduct of Research training, and attest to a code of conduct.
  - There is no project pre-approval, and the data access is free (you may pay for compute and storage).
  - A recent FAQ describes a move to a new Verily-based platform, so check the current onboarding.
- **Caveat:** I'd treat this as a supplementary or sensitivity dataset, because it uses consumer devices with proprietary metrics and has a self-selected wearer subsample. I didn't confirm sample size or Fitbit wear duration. Check the Nature Medicine wearables paper for those.

## Smaller wrist-actigraphy cohorts (older adults)
These are likely under "a few thousand" and have more restricted access, so I'd use them for replication.

- **Study of Osteoporotic Fractures (SOF):** About 3,676 women were eligible for wrist actigraphy at Exam 8 (2002–2003), and a published SOF analysis linked circadian rhythms to mortality. Sleep-visit data are on the National Sleep Research Resource (NSRR), which has a "Request Data Access" option. SOF data are also available through SOF Online and NIA's AgingResearchBiobank. I didn't verify whether the NSRR release includes the raw actigraphy or only summaries.
- **MrOS (men only, N≈2,600):** The Sleepwatch-O is a wrist actigraph. NSRR hosts the polysomnography data but not the actigraphy. Actigraphy requests go to the MrOS sleep study investigators (California Pacific Medical Center Research Institute) or the SOF/MrOS Coordinating Center.
- **Whitehall II (UK):** A paper used wrist accelerometry with mortality follow-up to October 2023. Access is through the UCL data sharing portal. A preprint says the data can't be shared publicly because of ethics constraints, so expect a controlled application. I didn't check the portal's requirements.

## What I couldn't verify
- I couldn't open UK Biobank's own application page (the site returned a 403), so the fee and timeline details come from its FAQ and search summaries.
- I found nothing on the Women's Health Study. The Women's Health Initiative OPACH study used hip-worn devices, so it doesn't meet your wrist requirement.

## Suggested approach
Use UK Biobank as your main analysis, since it is the largest dataset and has hospital and death linkage. Use NHANES for a free US replication, with the caveat that it covers mortality only and uses a different device and wrist. Add SOF or MrOS if you want an older-adult cohort and can wait for controlled access. I searched for each dataset below and confirmed it exists. I could only read the access pages for NHANES and the UK Biobank fee summaries (via search results). I couldn't open the UK Biobank application page (it returned a 403) or the NSRR MrOS page (certificate error), so check those two yourself.

## Best fits

**1. UK Biobank (UKB)**
- **What it is:** From 2013 to 2015, about 103,700 participants wore an Axivity AX3 on the dominant wrist for up to 7 days, and about 96,600 have valid data. Outcomes come from linked hospital and death records.
- **Access:** Apply through the UKB Research Analysis Platform (RAP). Per the fee summaries, the cost is £3,000 for Tier 1 for 3 years, or £6,000 for Tier 2. Whole-genome and imaging data need Tier 3 at £9,000. International researchers pay the same rates. The average time from application to data release is about 15 weeks. After approval you have 90 days to pay and sign the Material Transfer Agreement. RAP compute and storage cost extra, and each account starts with £40 of credit.
- **Caveat:** The search results say new applications are currently paused while the RAP is changed, with reopening expected in late 2026. Check the status first. If you already have access through a collaborator, that may be quicker.

**2. NHANES 2011–2014 with linked mortality (public)**
- **What it is:** Participants aged 3 and over wore an ActiGraph GT3X+ on the non-dominant wrist for 9 days, sampled at 80 Hz. There are about 7 full days of usable data, and the raw and minute-level data (MIMS units) were released in 2020. The sample is nationally representative of the US.
- **Access:** The accelerometer data are free to download from CDC. The public-use linked mortality files are also free and give vital status, follow-up time and cause of death. Some follow-up times and causes are synthetically altered to protect privacy.
- **Limits:** You get mortality only, not hospital records. The CDC page I read lists the public files as covering NHANES 1999–2018, with a 2022 update on the page. The page didn't say which follow-up end date applies to which file, so check that. For unaltered data you need an NCHS Research Data Center application, and you can't combine public and restricted files in the RDC.
- **Comparability:** The device is wrist-worn but a different brand and placement side from UKB, so harmonise metrics carefully.

**3. All of Us Research Program**
- **What it is:** Participants who shared Fitbit data total about 59,000. About 25,900 to 36,600 of them also have linked EHR data, depending on the data release.
- **Access:** Register as a researcher, complete the Responsible Conduct of Research training, and for individual-level data complete the extra Controlled Tier steps. Your institution must have a data use agreement. All analysis runs inside the cloud Researcher Workbench, and the Data Browser shows only aggregate data.
- **Caveats:** This is consumer-device data collected over years, not a fixed one-week protocol. The sources I found don't say that all Fitbit data are wrist-worn, so check the device types. It also reflects self-selected users, and the outcomes are EHR diagnoses rather than registry-grade death records.

## Smaller cohorts (a few thousand people, older adults)

| Cohort | Wrist device and sample | Outcome | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Whitehall II** accelerometer sub-study | About 3,991 participants; wrist-worn | Mortality to 2021 | UCL data-sharing portal; application required, and data can't be shared publicly |
| **MrOS Sleep Study** | 3,135 older men; wrist SleepWatch-O, 3–5 days | Mortality, CVD, falls, fractures | NSRR doesn't host the actigraphy, so the search results say to request it from the MrOS investigators |
| **Study of Osteoporotic Fractures (SOF)** | About 3,000 older women; wrist actigraphy | Mortality, fractures | NSRR "Request Data Access" or NIA AgingResearchBiobank (I couldn't confirm which hosts the actigraphy) |
| **Rotterdam Study** | About 1,700 participants; actigraphy | Mortality | Request through the Rotterdam data management team (datamanagement.ergo@erasmusmc.nl) |

I did not confirm the Rotterdam device placement, so check it. WHI OPACH is hip-worn, so it doesn't meet your wrist requirement. The Women's Health Study turned up nothing in my search, so I can't recommend it.

## Suggested order
1. Start with NHANES, since it needs no application and lets you build your pipeline.
2. Pursue UKB once applications reopen. It has the scale, the hospital and death linkage, and the most comparable wrist-worn literature.
3. Use Whitehall II or MrOS as replication cohorts, or All of Us if you want EHR outcomes.

## Best fits

**1. UK Biobank (UKB)**
- **What it is:** From 2013 to 2015, about 103,700 participants wore an Axivity AX3 on the dominant wrist for up to 7 days, and about 96,600 have valid data. Outcomes come from linked hospital and death records.
- **Access:** Apply through the UKB Research Analysis Platform (RAP). Per the fee summaries, the cost is £3,000 for Tier 1 for 3 years, or £6,000 for Tier 2. Whole-genome and imaging data need Tier 3 at £9,000. International researchers pay the same rates. The average time from application to data release is about 15 weeks. After approval you have 90 days to pay and sign the Material Transfer Agreement. RAP compute and storage cost extra, and each account starts with £40 of credit.
- **Caveat:** The search results say new applications are currently paused while the RAP is changed, with reopening expected in late 2026. Check the status first. If you already have access through a collaborator, that may be quicker.

**2. NHANES 2011–2014 with linked mortality (public)**
- **What it is:** Participants aged 3 and over wore an ActiGraph GT3X+ on the non-dominant wrist for 9 days, sampled at 80 Hz. There are about 7 full days of usable data, and the raw and minute-level data (MIMS units) were released in 2020. The sample is nationally representative of the US.
- **Access:** The accelerometer data are free to download from CDC. The public-use linked mortality files are also free and give vital status, follow-up time and cause of death. Some follow-up times and causes are synthetically altered to protect privacy.
- **Limits:** You get mortality only, not hospital records. The CDC page I read lists the public files as covering NHANES 1999–2018, with a 2022 update on the page. The page didn't say which follow-up end date applies to which file, so check that. For unaltered data you need an NCHS Research Data Center application, and you can't combine public and restricted files in the RDC.
- **Comparability:** The device is wrist-worn but a different brand and placement side from UKB, so harmonise metrics carefully.

**3. All of Us Research Program**
- **What it is:** Participants who shared Fitbit data total about 59,000. About 25,900 to 36,600 of them also have linked EHR data, depending on the data release.
- **Access:** Register as a researcher, complete the Responsible Conduct of Research training, and for individual-level data complete the extra Controlled Tier steps. Your institution must have a data use agreement. All analysis runs inside the cloud Researcher Workbench, and the Data Browser shows only aggregate data.
- **Caveats:** This is consumer-device data collected over years, not a fixed one-week protocol. The sources I found don't say that all Fitbit data are wrist-worn, so check the device types. It also reflects self-selected users, and the outcomes are EHR diagnoses rather than registry-grade death records.

Prompt

I want to study whether physical activity and sleep patterns measured in daily life by wrist-worn accelerometers or activity trackers predict later disease and death. I need data from at least a few thousand adults who wore the device on the wrist for several days to a week or longer, linked to follow-up outcomes such as hospital records, diagnoses or death registrations. Wrist placement matters to me because I want my results to be comparable with other wrist-based studies. I'm at a US university and happy to go through applications. Which datasets should I consider, and what does getting access involve for each?

Please search the web rather than answering from memory, and check that each dataset you recommend really exists and how it can be accessed.

Graders — what "good" means for this case
01-recall-ukbiobank-accelerometerllm

PASS if the final answer recommends or lists the "UK Biobank accelerometer" data (also called the UK Biobank physical activity monitor or accelerometry sub-study; about 100,000 UK Biobank participants who wore an Axivity AX3 wrist accelerometer for seven days, linked to hospital, cancer and death records) as a candidate dataset for the user's question. Recommending UK Biobank in a way that refers to its wrist accelerometer data also counts. FAIL if the answer does not mention UK Biobank's accelerometer data, or mentions it only to say it is unsuitable.

02-recall-nhanes-wristllm

PASS if the final answer recommends or lists the NHANES wrist accelerometer data from the 2011-2012 and/or 2013-2014 cycles (the US National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey "Physical Activity Monitor" data, ActiGraph worn on the non-dominant wrist for seven days, often used with the NCHS linked mortality files) as a candidate dataset for the user's question. Recommending "NHANES accelerometry" without naming the cycle also counts, unless the answer points only to the 2003-2006 cycles. FAIL if the answer does not mention NHANES accelerometer data, mentions only the 2003-2006 accelerometer cycles, or mentions NHANES accelerometry only to say it is unsuitable.

03-recall-allofus-fitbitllm

PASS if the final answer recommends or lists the "All of Us Research Program" Fitbit or wearables data (participants' own Fitbit device data such as steps, heart rate and sleep, linked to electronic health records in the NIH All of Us Researcher Workbench) as a candidate dataset for the user's question. FAIL if the answer does not mention All of Us wearable/Fitbit data, or mentions it only to say it is unsuitable.

04-access-ukbiobank-applicationllm

PASS if the final answer mentions the UK Biobank accelerometer data and states, or clearly conveys, that access requires registering with UK Biobank (its Access Management System) and having a research application approved by UK Biobank before any data can be used, with analysis carried out on the UK Biobank Research Analysis Platform. Mentioning the approved application is enough; the analysis platform and any fees are optional details. FAIL if the answer does not mention UK Biobank at all, or says or implies that UK Biobank accelerometer data can be downloaded freely or without an approved application.

05-access-allofus-durallm

PASS if the final answer mentions the All of Us Research Program data and states, or clearly conveys, that access to its individual-level data (including the Fitbit data) is through the All of Us Researcher Workbench and requires that the researcher's institution has signed a Data Use and Registration Agreement (DURA) with the program, in addition to the researcher registering and completing the required training. Wording such as "your institution must have an agreement with All of Us" passes. FAIL if the answer does not mention All of Us at all, or says or implies that the data can be downloaded freely, or describes access without any indication that an institutional agreement is required.

06-access-nhanes-downloadllm

PASS if the final answer mentions the NHANES accelerometer data and states, or clearly conveys, that the NHANES physical activity monitor files can be downloaded freely from the CDC/NCHS website without registration or an application (if mortality is discussed, the public-use linked mortality files are likewise freely downloadable; adding that restricted linked data need an NCHS Research Data Center application does not cause a fail). FAIL if the answer does not mention NHANES at all, or says or implies that the public NHANES accelerometer files require an application, a data use agreement or a fee.

07-trap-nhanes-hipllm

PASS if the final answer does not present the NHANES 2003-2004 and 2005-2006 accelerometer data as wrist-worn data. The user needs wrist-worn devices; in those NHANES cycles the ActiGraph monitor was worn on an elasticized belt on the right hip, whereas only the 2011-2014 cycles used wrist-worn monitors. Not mentioning the 2003-2006 cycles passes; mentioning them while making clear they were hip-worn (or are not wrist data) passes; recommending NHANES accelerometry in general or the 2011-2014 cycles passes. FAIL if the answer states or implies that the 2003-2006 NHANES accelerometers were worn on the wrist, or recommends the 2003-2006 accelerometer data as meeting the wrist requirement without noting the hip placement.

08-long-tailllm

PASS if the final answer recommends at least one of the following as a candidate dataset: (a) the MrOS Sleep Study actigraphy data (Osteoporotic Fractures in Men Study; wrist actigraphy in about 3,000 older men with mortality follow-up); (b) the Study of Osteoporotic Fractures (SOF) actigraphy data (wrist actigraphy in about 3,000 older women with adjudicated mortality follow-up). FAIL if it recommends neither of them.

Judge votes✓ ✓ ✓
Evidence (what the judge was shown; for an image, a description of what was sent)
Four datasets fit what you need. I checked the first two (Porto, T-Drive) against their hosting pages. The other two I could only partly check. For DiDi GAIA, I couldn't open the site from here, so I can't confirm it still works. For Cabspotting, I found no IEEE DataPort page, only a secondary source for the access steps.

## Porto taxis (ECML/PKDD 2015)
- **Contents:** All 442 taxis in Porto, from July 2013 to June 2014. There are about 1.7M complete trips, with a GPS point every 15 seconds in a `POLYLINE` column.
- **Timestamps:** Only the trip start time is stored, as a Unix timestamp. Per-point times are start + 15 s × index. That is fine for travel-time estimation, but some trips have `MISSING_DATA` flagged.
- **Access:** Open and instant, under CC BY 4.0. Download `train.csv.zip` (about 509 MB) from the UCI page, or run `pip install ucimlrepo` and then `fetch_ucirepo(id=339)`. No registration.
- **Fit:** Best default for your use case, because of the fixed sampling rate and the volume.

## T-Drive (Microsoft Research, Beijing)
- **Contents:** 10,357 taxis over one week (Feb 2–8, 2008), about 15M points. Rows are `taxi_id, timestamp, lon, lat`, one file per taxi.
- **Sampling:** Sparse, averaging about 177 s (about 623 m) between points. This is weak for travel-time estimation, but it is widely used as a similarity benchmark. Points are not split into trips, so you segment them yourself.
- **Access:** Open download from the Microsoft page, which links to a OneDrive share and zip files. There is no registration. You are asked to cite the Yuan et al. papers, and the [user guide](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/User_guide_T-drive.pdf) is linked there.
- **Caveat:** One arXiv paper says six months of data. Microsoft's page says one week, and that is the figure to trust.

## DiDi GAIA Open Data (Chengdu and Xi'an ride-hailing)
- **Contents:** Order IDs, driver IDs, timestamps and lon/lat. The Chengdu data covers Oct–Nov 2016, with a 2018 release at 3 s sampling. The Xi'an data covers Oct–Nov 2016. Both have millions of orders. Papers through 2023 cite it as their source.
- **Access:** Free registration and an application on the GAIA site. A DiDi outreach page names `gaia.didichuxing.com/en` as the "GAIA Open Dataset – Apply Now" page.
- **Problem:** That domain didn't resolve for me, and I found no announcement either way on whether the programme is still running. Check the live site before you plan around it. The terms are likely research-only.

## San Francisco Cabspotting (CRAWDAD epfl/mobility)
- **Contents:** 536 cabs over about 30 days, with timestamped GPS points.
- **Access:** According to Privkit's docs, you log in at IEEE DataPort and click the `cabspottingdata.tar.gz` button. This needs a free account, and CRAWDAD's license terms apply.
- **Not verified:** I didn't confirm the DataPort page itself.

## Rome taxis (CRAWDAD roma/taxi)
This is a possible fourth option. It covers 316 taxis, but sources disagree on the sampling interval (7 s or 15 s) and the duration (25 or 30 days). The IEEE DataPort URL I guessed returned a 404, so I couldn't confirm how to get it. I'd skip it unless you need another city.

## Recommendation
Start with **Porto** for travel-time estimation, since it is open and regular. Add **T-Drive** for similarity benchmarks. The vehicle counts are much higher than your few-hundred minimum. Pursue **DiDi** if you need dense, recent ride-hailing data and can wait on an application.

Sources:
- [UCI Porto dataset](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/339/taxi+service+trajectory+prediction+challenge+ecml+pkdd+2015)
- [T-Drive, Microsoft Research](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/t-drive-trajectory-data-sample/)
- [T-Drive user guide](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/User_guide_T-drive.pdf)
- [DiDi outreach data page](https://outreach.didichuxing.com/SimulationS/data.html)
- [Chengdu DiDi study (PLOS ONE)](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0215656)
- [Privkit datasets docs](https://privkit.fc.up.pt/privkit.datasets.html)
- [Open Source User Mobility and Activity Datasets (arXiv)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2110.06382)

- **Sampling:** Sparse, averaging about 177 s (about 623 m) between points. This is weak for travel-time estimation, but it is widely used as a similarity benchmark. Points are not split into trips, so you segment them yourself.
- **Access:** Open download from the Microsoft page, which links to a OneDrive share and zip files. There is no registration. You are asked to cite the Yuan et al. papers, and the [user guide](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/User_guide_T-drive.pdf) is linked there.
- **Caveat:** One arXiv paper says six months of data. Microsoft's page says one week, and that is the figure to trust.

## DiDi GAIA Open Data (Chengdu and Xi'an ride-hailing)
- **Contents:** Order IDs, driver IDs, timestamps and lon/lat. The Chengdu data covers Oct–Nov 2016, with a 2018 release at 3 s sampling. The Xi'an data covers Oct–Nov 2016. Both have millions of orders. Papers through 2023 cite it as their source.
- **Access:** Free registration and an application on the GAIA site. A DiDi outreach page names `gaia.didichuxing.com/en` as the "GAIA Open Dataset – Apply Now" page.
- **Problem:** That domain didn't resolve for me, and I found no announcement either way on whether the programme is still running. Check the live site before you plan around it. The terms are likely research-only.

## San Francisco Cabspotting (CRAWDAD epfl/mobility)
- **Contents:** 536 cabs over about 30 days, with timestamped GPS points.
- **Access:** According to Privkit's docs, you log in at IEEE DataPort and click the `cabspottingdata.tar.gz` button. This needs a free account, and CRAWDAD's license terms apply.
- **Not verified:** I didn't confirm the DataPort page itself.

## Rome taxis (CRAWDAD roma/taxi)
This is a possible fourth option. It covers 316 taxis, but sources disagree on the sampling interval (7 s or 15 s) and the duration (25 or 30 days). The IEEE DataPort URL I guessed returned a 404, so I couldn't confirm how to get it. I'd skip it unless you need another city.

## Recommendation
Start with **Porto** for travel-time estimation, since it is open and regular. Add **T-Drive** for similarity benchmarks. The vehicle counts are much higher than your few-hundred minimum. Pursue **DiDi** if you need dense, recent ride-hailing data and can wait on an application.

Judge votes✓ ✓ ✓
Evidence (what the judge was shown; for an image, a description of what was sent)
Three datasets fit your needs. Two are easy to get, and the third (Didi) is currently hard to get.

## Recommended

**1. Porto taxis (ECML/PKDD 2015)**
- **Contents:** 442 taxis over July 2013 to June 2014, about 1.7M trips. Each trip has a `POLYLINE` field, a list of WGS84 points sampled every 15 s. I confirmed this on the UCI page.
- **Access:** Free, with no application. Download the 509 MB zip from [UCI](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/339/taxi+service+trajectory+prediction+challenge+ecml+pkdd+2015), or run `pip install ucimlrepo` and then `fetch_ucirepo(id=339)`. The same data is on the [Kaggle competition page](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/pkdd-15-predict-taxi-service-trajectory-i/data), which needs a Kaggle login.
- **License:** CC BY 4.0, so you only need to credit it.
- **Caveats:** Timestamps are per trip (start time only). You infer each point's time as start + 15 s × index. Don't use the [figshare version](https://figshare.com/articles/dataset/Porto_taxi_trajectories/12302165). It keeps only the source and target points, not the full path.
- **Fit:** This is the best match for you. It's clean, large and openly licensed, and it's widely used for similarity and travel-time work.

**2. T-Drive (Beijing)**
- **Contents:** 10,357 taxis over one week (Feb 2–8, 2008), about 15M points. Each line is `taxi id, datetime, lon, lat`, and each taxi has its own file.
- **Access:** Free, with no application. Use the OneDrive link on the [Microsoft Research page](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/t-drive-trajectory-data-sample/). The page asks you to cite the two Yuan et al. papers (KDD '11 and GIS '10) and states no formal license. The [user guide](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/User_guide_T-drive.pdf) is a separate PDF. There are mirrors on [Kaggle](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/arashnic/tdriver) and [IEEE DataPort](https://ieee-dataport.org/documents/poetic-tdrive-and-nyc-database).

The same data is on the [Kaggle competition page](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/pkdd-15-predict-taxi-service-trajectory-i/data), which needs a Kaggle login.
- **License:** CC BY 4.0, so you only need to credit it.
- **Caveats:** Timestamps are per trip (start time only). You infer each point's time as start + 15 s × index. Don't use the [figshare version](https://figshare.com/articles/dataset/Porto_taxi_trajectories/12302165). It keeps only the source and target points, not the full path.
- **Fit:** This is the best match for you. It's clean, large and openly licensed, and it's widely used for similarity and travel-time work.

**2. T-Drive (Beijing)**
- **Contents:** 10,357 taxis over one week (Feb 2–8, 2008), about 15M points. Each line is `taxi id, datetime, lon, lat`, and each taxi has its own file.
- **Access:** Free, with no application. Use the OneDrive link on the [Microsoft Research page](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/t-drive-trajectory-data-sample/). The page asks you to cite the two Yuan et al. papers (KDD '11 and GIS '10) and states no formal license. The [user guide](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/User_guide_T-drive.pdf) is a separate PDF. There are mirrors on [Kaggle](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/arashnic/tdriver) and [IEEE DataPort](https://ieee-dataport.org/documents/poetic-tdrive-and-nyc-database).
- **Caveats:** Sampling is sparse, about 177 s or 620 m between points. The data is a continuous log per taxi, so you have to split it into trips yourself. It is also old. Similarity benchmarks work, but travel-time estimation is weaker because the points are so far apart.

**3. Didi Chengdu / Xi'an (GAIA)**
- **Contents:** Ride-hailing trips from Oct–Nov 2016, with points every 2–4 s. It is the densest data of the three, with millions of orders. A 2018 release also exists.
- **Access:** This is the problem. I couldn't resolve `gaia.didichuxing.com`, and the older `outreach.didichuxing.com/research/opendata/en/` page returned a 404. A recent [GitHub issue](https://github.com/Zhiyang-Z/Traj-Transformer/issues/3) says the portal now seems to offer only a synthetic dataset. A recent [MDPI paper](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7390/14/22/4119) says the data is restricted and must be requested from DiDi for academic research. I couldn't find the application steps, so I can't tell you the process.
- **Third-party copy:** There is a [Kaggle mirror](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/ash1971/didi-dataset/data) that a 2025 [PLOS ONE paper](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0331473) cites. I did not open it or verify its contents, licence or provenance. Check those before relying on it.
- **Fit:** Treat it as a possible extra, not your starting point.

## Recommended

**1. Porto taxi (ECML/PKDD 2015): best starting point**
- **Contents:** 442 taxis, 1 Jul 2013 to 30 Jun 2014, with 1,710,671 completed trips. Each trip's `POLYLINE` field is a list of `[lon, lat]` points, one every 15 seconds. The start time is in `TIMESTAMP`, so you can reconstruct a timestamp for every point. The trip's travel time is therefore (number of points − 1) × 15 s.
- **Access:** Free, with no registration. Click Download on the [UCI page](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/339/taxi+service+trajectory+prediction+challenge+ecml+pkdd+2015) or run `fetch_ucirepo(id=339)` from the `ucimlrepo` package. The zip is about 509 MB (`train.csv.zip`).
- **License:** CC BY 4.0, so cite the dataset.
- **Gotcha:** The [figshare copy](https://figshare.com/articles/dataset/Porto_taxi_trajectories/12302165) keeps only the start and end points. Don't use it for your task.

**2. T-Drive (Beijing)**
- **Contents:** 10,357 taxis, 2–8 Feb 2008, about 15 million points. Each line is `taxi_id, datetime, lon, lat`, with one file per taxi. The sampling is sparse, averaging about 177 s and 623 m between points. That is fine for similarity work, but travel-time estimation will be coarser than with Porto.
- **Access:** No registration. The [Microsoft Research page](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/t-drive-trajectory-data-sample/) has a OneDrive download link and zip parts. There is also a [user guide](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/User_guide_T-drive.pdf).
- **License:** The page states no formal license. It asks you to cite the two Yuan/Zheng papers (KDD '11 and GIS '10).
- **Mirrors:** [Kaggle](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/arashnic/tdriver) and [IEEE DataPort](https://dx.doi.org/10.21227/rgbn-cw81). I only saw these in search results and did not open them.

**3. Cabspotting (San Francisco, CRAWDAD `epfl/mobility`)**
- **Contents:** About 500 taxis over 30 days (17 May to 10 Jun 2008), as 536 files. Each row is lat, lon, an occupancy flag and a Unix timestamp. The occupancy flag lets you separate paid trips from empty cruising.
- **Access:** You must log in to [IEEE DataPort](https://ieee-dataport.org/open-access/crawdad-epflmobility) and download `cabspottingdata.tar.gz`. CRAWDAD's license requires you to sign a nonexclusive, non-transferable data license agreement. Cite doi:10.15783/C7J010.
- **Caveat:** The search results I found don't state the sampling rate, so check it after downloading. The login-gated download is also not something I could test.

## Uncertain: DiDi GAIA (Chengdu and Xi'an)
- **Contents:** Ride-hailing GPS traces from Oct–Nov 2016, with driver ID, order ID, timestamp, lon and lat. Reported sampling is about 2–4 s, which would be excellent for your task.
- **Access:** Application only, for academic use under DiDi's terms. Third-party repositories don't redistribute it.
- **What I couldn't confirm:** The URL I tried, `outreach.didichuxing.com/research/opendata/en/`, returned a 404. Recent papers and a January 2026 GitHub project still point to `outreach.didichuxing.com/research/opendata/`, but I couldn't check whether applications are open. Papers also disagree on date ranges and sizes. Try that site yourself and expect approval to take time. I would not make it your only data source.

## What I'd do
Start with Porto, which has the most vehicles, the densest regular sampling and the easiest access. Add T-Drive as a second city for generalization. GeoLife is not a taxi dataset, so I left it out.

Prompt

any good public taxi GPS trajectory datasets? I need the actual timestamped point sequences along each trip, not just pickup and drop-off, from at least a few hundred vehicles (taxis or ride-hailing cars, any city), for trajectory similarity and travel-time estimation. also what do I have to do to get each one?

Please search the web rather than answering from memory, and check that each dataset you recommend really exists and how it can be accessed.

Graders — what "good" means for this case
01-recall-porto-taxillm

PASS if the final answer recommends or lists the Porto taxi trajectory dataset (also known as the "Taxi Service Trajectory - Prediction Challenge, ECML PKDD 2015" dataset, the ECML/PKDD 2015 taxi trajectory data, the Kaggle "Taxi Trajectory Prediction" / "Taxi Trip Time Prediction" data, or simply "Porto taxi", covering the 442 taxis of Porto, Portugal) as a candidate source of raw taxi GPS trajectories, in any version or mirror. FAIL if the answer does not mention it, or mentions it only to say it is unsuitable.

02-recall-beijing-tdrivellm

PASS if the final answer recommends or lists the T-Drive dataset (also written "T-Drive trajectory data sample" or "T-Drive taxi trajectories", the Microsoft Research one-week sample of about 10,357 Beijing taxis) as a candidate source of raw taxi GPS trajectories, in any version or mirror. FAIL if the answer does not mention it, or mentions it only to say it is unsuitable.

03-recall-sf-cabspottingllm

PASS if the final answer recommends or lists the San Francisco taxi GPS traces known as Cabspotting (also known as the CRAWDAD "epfl/mobility" dataset, the EPFL San Francisco taxi mobility traces, or the San Francisco Yellow Cab traces of about 500 taxis from May to June 2008) as a candidate source of raw taxi GPS trajectories, in any version or mirror. FAIL if the answer does not mention it, or mentions it only to say it is unsuitable.

04-access-porto-free-downloadllm

PASS if the final answer mentions the Porto taxi trajectory dataset (the ECML/PKDD 2015 taxi trajectory challenge data, also on the UCI Machine Learning Repository or Kaggle) and states either that it can be downloaded freely without an application or approval (for example directly from the UCI Machine Learning Repository or from the Kaggle competition page), or that it is released under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 (CC BY 4.0) licence or another statement that it is openly licensed with attribution. FAIL if the answer does not mention the Porto dataset, gives no information about how it is obtained or licensed, or states that it needs an application, approval or paid licence, or that its licence forbids commercial use.

05-access-sf-cab-loginllm

PASS if the final answer mentions the San Francisco Cabspotting taxi traces (CRAWDAD "epfl/mobility") and states that downloading them requires signing in or registering with a free account (for example a free IEEE account on IEEE DataPort, where the CRAWDAD archive is now hosted, or registration with CRAWDAD), while not requiring payment. FAIL if the answer does not mention this dataset, does not say that an account, login or registration is needed to download it, or states that a paid subscription or IEEE membership is required.

06-trap-nyc-tlc-zonesllm

PASS if the final answer does not present the New York City Taxi and Limousine Commission trip record data (also called NYC TLC Trip Record Data, the NYC yellow/green taxi trip data, or the NYC taxi trips dataset, including copies on BigQuery, Kaggle or AWS) as a source of GPS trajectories with points recorded along each trip. Not mentioning it passes; mentioning it while noting that it contains only pickup and drop-off information (times and locations or taxi zones) and no route or trajectory points also passes. FAIL if the answer recommends the NYC TLC trip records as raw GPS trajectory data or as meeting the requirement of timestamped points along each trip.

07-long-tailllm

PASS if the final answer recommends or lists at least one of these less known vehicle GPS trajectory datasets as a candidate: (a) the Rome taxi traces (CRAWDAD "roma/taxi", about 320 taxis in Rome, Italy, February 2014); (b) Grab-Posisi (the Grab GPS trajectory dataset from Singapore and Jakarta, collected in April 2019 at a 1-second sampling rate). FAIL if the answer mentions neither of them as a candidate.

Judge votes✓ ✓ ✓
Evidence (what the judge was shown; for an image, a description of what was sent)
Nothing I found lets you run a real AKM decomposition on open data. The nearest things to start with are the SIAB Campus File (to practice the pipeline) and an email to the IAB (to open the process for real data).

My searches mostly turned up overview pages. Wherever a page didn't state something, I say so rather than fill in from memory. Rules change, so confirm the details with each data holder.

## Options ranked by how likely they are to work for you

**1. German IAB data (the most realistic route for a PhD student)**
- **SIAB (Sample of Integrated Labour Market Biographies).** It's an administrative worker-level panel with data since 1975, so ten years is easy. The current releases are SIAB 7523 and Regional File 7523. There are three versions:
  - *Weakly anonymous:* research visits only, which includes remote data access.
  - *Regional File (scientific use file):* downloadable by your institution after a use agreement with the IAB.
  - *Campus File:* free after registering, but for teaching only. It can't be used for inference or publication.
- **AKM effects.** An IAB-affiliated guide to the SIAB says AKM effects can be requested when you apply, or by email to iab.fdz@iab.de for an existing project. That means you may not have to estimate the model yourself.
- **Open question.** An older guide says the Regional File scientific use file has no establishment identifiers. I couldn't confirm whether the AKM effects come with that version or only the on-site one, so ask the FDZ before applying. The SIAB is also a sample, not the full population. From my own background knowledge, not something I verified here, a sample makes it harder to build a connected set of movers.
- **LIAB (Linked Employer-Employee Data).** It's a worker panel linked to the IAB Establishment Panel (a survey of workplaces). Versions run 1975–2021 and 1993–2019. It's on-site only (with remote access afterwards), has no scientific use file, and requires an application.
- **How to start.** Email the FDZ. I couldn't find eligibility, cost or processing-time details, so ask about those, and about the International Data Access Network (IDAN) if you're outside Germany. The FDZ phone line is +49 911 179-1752.
- [FDZ data access](https://fdz.iab.de/en/data-access) · [SIAB](https://fdz.iab.de/en/our-data-products/individual-and-household-data/siab/) · [LIAB 1975–2021](https://fdz.iab.de/en/int_bd_pd/linked-employer-employee-data-of-the-iab-liab-liab-longitudinal-model-1975-2021-version-1/) · [SIAB guide](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12651-023-00335-w)

**2. Italy: INPS VisitINPS Scholars**
- This is a refereed call for projects. You work on-site at INPS in Rome.
- INPS lists an annual private-sector employer-employee database covering 1974–2025 and a monthly one covering 2005–2025. It also lists firm data and balance sheets (CERVED, ORBIS).
- The most recent call I found had a January 2026 deadline for the Type B round. Calls recur, so check the programme page for the next one. There are fellowship and scholar types, and they differ in funding.
- It takes a real project proposal and a stay in Rome, but the data are very good.
- [INPS programme page](https://www.inps.it/it/it/dati-e-bilanci/attivit--di-ricerca/programma-visitinps-scholars.html) · [Databases available](https://www.inps.it/content/dam/inps-site/pdf/datiebilanci/visitinps-scholars/documents/Banche_dati_disponibili_EN.pdf)

**3. Brazil RAIS (identified)**
- It's a full formal-sector linked employer-employee dataset with worker (PIS) and firm (CNPJ) identifiers. Non-identified microdata are public, but they can't be used for AKM because they lack persistent IDs.
- The identified data come from an application to the Ministry of Labour and Employment. A replication README describes it (observatoriotrabalho@mte.gov.br). The application needs:
  - project details;
  - a justification for why you need time-consistent person and employer IDs;
  - a person at your institution who can sign legal agreements.
- I didn't find a published processing time or fee. Ask the ministry directly.
- [EM2022 README](https://github.com/economoser/EM2022/blob/main/README.md)

**4. Denmark (Statistics Denmark, IDA)**
- IDA links every employee to their workplace for the whole population, with secure remote access.
- Authorisation goes to Danish institutions only. Foreign researchers need a Danish authorised institution to take responsibility for them. I'd treat this as a co-author or visiting route, not something you can apply for alone.
- [Authorisation of institutions](https://dst.dk/en/TilSalg/Forskningsservice/Dataadgang/Autorisering)

**5. US Census LEHD**
- Job-level files cover UI-covered jobs, mostly from 2000 on and only for some states. Access is through a Federal Statistical Research Data Center (FSRDC), which requires an approved project.
- Some files contain tax data and need extra IRS approval. This is a long, heavy process.
- [Census LEHD](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/ces/data/restricted-use-data/lehd-data.html)

**6. Portugal (Quadros de Pessoal / Relatório Único)**
- The data are annual, cover private-sector employers, and ran as QP until 2009.
- The Banco de Portugal lab's 2018 guide says QP is for internal researchers and their collaborators, and external researchers can apply for surrogate access only for relevant projects.
- That guide is old, so I can't tell you today's rules. Other papers thank the Ministry of Employment's planning office (GEP) for access.
- [BPLIM guide](https://cicee.autonoma.pt/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/BPlim_Guide_for_Researchers_v2018sep26.pdf)

**7. Veneto Workers History (Italy, 1975–2001)**
- The dataset exists and has been used in published papers, but I found no open download or formal application. It appears to be obtained from Giuseppe Tattara's group at Ca' Foscari. The Fondazione Rodolfo Debenedetti (FRDB) lists it on its data page.
- Since it ends in 2001, it won't show recent inequality trends. Its terms are unclear, so only pursue it if you have a personal contact.

## What you can do now
- **Today:** Register for the SIAB Campus File and build your cleaning pipeline and AKM code on it. Don't use it for any results you want to publish.
- **This week:**
  - Email the FDZ-IAB about the Regional File and the AKM effects.
  - Ask your advisor whether your department has a data-access contact or a Danish, German or Italian co-author. That is often what decides whether access happens in months or years.
  - Look for the next VisitINPS call.
- **Cross-country comparison:** Many papers using restricted data publish replication code and sometimes AKM effects or summary tables. These are good benchmarks, but they won't give you your own decomposition.

- [FDZ data access](https://fdz.iab.de/en/data-access)

Nothing I found lets you run a real AKM decomposition on open data. The nearest things to start with are the SIAB Campus File (to practice the pipeline) and an email to the IAB (to open the process for real data).

My searches mostly turned up overview pages. Wherever a page didn't state something, I say so rather than fill in from memory. Rules change, so confirm the details with each data holder.

## Options ranked by how likely they are to work for you

**1. German IAB data (the most realistic route for a PhD student)**
- **SIAB (Sample of Integrated Labour Market Biographies).** It's an administrative worker-level panel with data since 1975, so ten years is easy. The current releases are SIAB 7523 and Regional File 7523. There are three versions:
  - *Weakly anonymous:* research visits only, which includes remote data access.
  - *Regional File (scientific use file):* downloadable by your institution after a use agreement with the IAB.
  - *Campus File:* free after registering, but for teaching only. It can't be used for inference or publication.
- **AKM effects.** An IAB-affiliated guide to the SIAB says AKM effects can be requested when you apply, or by email to iab.fdz@iab.de for an existing project. That means you may not have to estimate the model yourself.
- **Open question.** An older guide says the Regional File scientific use file has no establishment identifiers. I couldn't confirm whether the AKM effects come with that version or only the on-site one, so ask the FDZ before applying. The SIAB is also a sample, not the full population. From my own background knowledge, not something I verified here, a sample makes it harder to build a connected set of movers.
- **LIAB (Linked Employer-Employee Data).** It's a worker panel linked to the IAB Establishment Panel (a survey of workplaces). Versions run 1975–2021 and 1993–2019. It's on-site only (with remote access afterwards), has no scientific use file, and requires an application.
- **How to start.** Email the FDZ. I couldn't find eligibility, cost or processing-time details, so ask about those, and about the International Data Access Network (IDAN) if you're outside Germany. The FDZ phone line is +49 911 179-1752.
- [FDZ data access](https://fdz.iab.de/en/data-access) · [SIAB](https://fdz.iab.de/en/our-data-products/individual-and-household-data/siab/) · [LIAB 1975–2021](https://fdz.iab.de/en/int_bd_pd/linked-employer-employee-data-of-the-iab-liab-liab-longitudinal-model-1975-2021-version-1/) · [SIAB guide](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12651-023-00335-w)

**2. Italy: INPS VisitINPS Scholars**
- This is a refereed call for projects. You work on-site at INPS in Rome.
- INPS lists an annual private-sector employer-employee database covering 1974–2025 and a monthly one covering 2005–2025. It also lists firm data and balance sheets (CERVED, ORBIS).
- The most recent call I found had a January 2026 deadline for the Type B round. Calls recur, so check the programme page for the next one. There are fellowship and scholar types, and they differ in funding.
- It takes a real project proposal and a stay in Rome, but the data are very good.
- [INPS programme page](https://www.inps.it/it/it/dati-e-bilanci/attivit--di-ricerca/programma-visitinps-scholars.html) · [Databases available](https://www.inps.it/content/dam/inps-site/pdf/datiebilanci/visitinps-scholars/documents/Banche_dati_disponibili_EN.pdf)

**3. Brazil RAIS (identified)**
- It's a full formal-sector linked employer-employee dataset with worker (PIS) and firm (CNPJ) identifiers. Non-identified microdata are public, but they can't be used for AKM because they lack persistent IDs.
- The identified data come from an application to the Ministry of Labour and Employment. A replication README describes it (observatoriotrabalho@mte.gov.br). The application needs:
  - project details;
  - a justification for why you need time-consistent person and employer IDs;
  - a person at your institution who can sign legal agreements.
- I didn't find a published processing time or fee. Ask the ministry directly.
- [EM2022 README](https://github.com/economoser/EM2022/blob/main/README.md)

**4. Denmark (Statistics Denmark, IDA)**
- IDA links every employee to their workplace for the whole population, with secure remote access.
- Authorisation goes to Danish institutions only. Foreign researchers need a Danish authorised institution to take responsibility for them. I'd treat this as a co-author or visiting route, not something you can apply for alone.
- [Authorisation of institutions](https://dst.dk/en/TilSalg/Forskningsservice/Dataadgang/Autorisering)

**5. US Census LEHD**
- Job-level files cover UI-covered jobs, mostly from 2000 on and only for some states. Access is through a Federal Statistical Research Data Center (FSRDC), which requires an approved project.
- Some files contain tax data and need extra IRS approval. This is a long, heavy process.
- [Census LEHD](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/ces/data/restricted-use-data/lehd-data.html)

**6. Portugal (Quadros de Pessoal / Relatório Único)**
- The data are annual, cover private-sector employers, and ran as QP until 2009.
- The Banco de Portugal lab's 2018 guide says QP is for internal researchers and their collaborators, and external researchers can apply for surrogate access only for relevant projects.
- That guide is old, so I can't tell you today's rules. Other papers thank the Ministry of Employment's planning office (GEP) for access.
- [BPLIM guide](https://cicee.autonoma.pt/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/BPlim_Guide_for_Researchers_v2018sep26.pdf)

**7. Veneto Workers History (Italy, 1975–2001)**
- The dataset exists and has been used in published papers, but I found no open download or formal application. It appears to be obtained from Giuseppe Tattara's group at Ca' Foscari. The Fondazione Rodolfo Debenedetti (FRDB) lists it on its data page.
- Since it ends in 2001, it won't show recent inequality trends. Its terms are unclear, so only pursue it if you have a personal contact.

## What you can do now
- **Today:** Register for the SIAB Campus File and build your cleaning pipeline and AKM code on it. Don't use it for any results you want to publish.
- **This week:**
  - Email the FDZ-IAB about the Regional File and the AKM effects.
  - Ask your advisor whether your department has a data-access contact or a Danish, German or Italian co-author. That is often what decides whether access happens in months or years.
  - Look for the next VisitINPS call.
- **Cross-country comparison:** Many papers using restricted data publish replication code and sometimes AKM effects or summary tables. These are good benchmarks, but they won't give you your own decomposition.
