- **LIAB (Linked Employer-Employee Data).** It's a worker panel linked to the IAB Establishment Panel (a survey of workplaces). Versions run 1975–2021 and 1993–2019. It's on-site only (with remote access afterwards), has no scientific use file, and requires an application.
- **How to start.** Email the FDZ. I couldn't find eligibility, cost or processing-time details, so ask about those, and about the International Data Access Network (IDAN) if you're outside Germany. The FDZ phone line is +49 911 179-1752.
- [FDZ data access](https://fdz.iab.de/en/data-access) · [SIAB](https://fdz.iab.de/en/our-data-products/individual-and-household-data/siab/) · [LIAB 1975–2021](https://fdz.iab.de/en/int_bd_pd/linked-employer-employee-data-of-the-iab-liab-liab-longitudinal-model-1975-2021-version-1/) · [SIAB guide](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12651-023-00335-w)

**2. Italy: INPS VisitINPS Scholars**
- This is a refereed call for projects. You work on-site at INPS in Rome.
- INPS lists an annual private-sector employer-employee database covering 1974–2025 and a monthly one covering 2005–2025. It also lists firm data and balance sheets (CERVED, ORBIS).
- The most recent call I found had a January 2026 deadline for the Type B round. Calls recur, so check the programme page for the next one. There are fellowship and scholar types, and they differ in funding.
- It takes a real project proposal and a stay in Rome, but the data are very good.
- [INPS programme page](https://www.inps.it/it/it/dati-e-bilanci/attivit--di-ricerca/programma-visitinps-scholars.html) · [Databases available](https://www.inps.it/content/dam/inps-site/pdf/datiebilanci/visitinps-scholars/documents/Banche_dati_disponibili_EN.pdf)

**3. Brazil RAIS (identified)**
- It's a full formal-sector linked employer-employee dataset with worker (PIS) and firm (CNPJ) identifiers. Non-identified microdata are public, but they can't be used for AKM because they lack persistent IDs.
- The identified data come from an application to the Ministry of Labour and Employment. A replication README describes it (observatoriotrabalho@mte.gov.br). The application needs:
  - project details;
  - a justification for why you need time-consistent person and employer IDs;
  - a person at your institution who can sign legal agreements.
- I didn't find a published processing time or fee. Ask the ministry directly.
- [EM2022 README](https://github.com/economoser/EM2022/blob/main/README.md)

**4. Denmark (Statistics Denmark, IDA)**
- IDA links every employee to their workplace for the whole population, with secure remote access.
- Authorisation goes to Danish institutions only. Foreign researchers need a Danish authorised institution to take responsibility for them. I'd treat this as a co-author or visiting route, not something you can apply for alone.
- [Authorisation of institutions](https://dst.dk/en/TilSalg/Forskningsservice/Dataadgang/Autorisering)

**5. US Census LEHD**
- Job-level files cover UI-covered jobs, mostly from 2000 on and only for some states. Access is through a Federal Statistical Research Data Center (FSRDC), which requires an approved project.
- Some files contain tax data and need extra IRS approval. This is a long, heavy process.
- [Census LEHD](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/ces/data/restricted-use-data/lehd-data.html)

**6. Portugal (Quadros de Pessoal / Relatório Único)**
- The data are annual, cover private-sector employers, and ran as QP until 2009.
- The Banco de Portugal lab's 2018 guide says QP is for internal researchers and their collaborators, and external researchers can apply for surrogate access only for relevant projects.
- That guide is old, so I can't tell you today's rules. Other papers thank the Ministry of Employment's planning office (GEP) for access.
- [BPLIM guide](https://cicee.autonoma.pt/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/BPlim_Guide_for_Researchers_v2018sep26.pdf)

**7. Veneto Workers History (Italy, 1975–2001)**
- The dataset exists and has been used in published papers, but I found no open download or formal application. It appears to be obtained from Giuseppe Tattara's group at Ca' Foscari. The Fondazione Rodolfo Debenedetti (FRDB) lists it on its data page.
- Since it ends in 2001, it won't show recent inequality trends. Its terms are unclear, so only pursue it if you have a personal contact.

## What you can do now
- **Today:** Register for the SIAB Campus File and build your cleaning pipeline and AKM code on it. Don't use it for any results you want to publish.
- **This week:**
  - Email the FDZ-IAB about the Regional File and the AKM effects.
  - Ask your advisor whether your department has a data-access contact or a Danish, German or Italian co-author. That is often what decides whether access happens in months or years.
  - Look for the next VisitINPS call.
- **Cross-country comparison:** Many papers using restricted data publish replication code and sometimes AKM effects or summary tables. These are good benchmarks, but they won't give you your own decomposition.

- The Banco de Portugal lab's 2018 guide says QP is for internal researchers and their collaborators, and external researchers can apply for surrogate access only for relevant projects.
- That guide is old, so I can't tell you today's rules. Other papers thank the Ministry of Employment's planning office (GEP) for access.
- [BPLIM guide](https://cicee.autonoma.pt/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/BPlim_Guide_for_Researchers_v2018sep26.pdf)

**7. Veneto Workers History (Italy, 1975–2001)**
- The dataset exists and has been used in published papers, but I found no open download or formal application. It appears to be obtained from Giuseppe Tattara's group at Ca' Foscari. The Fondazione Rodolfo Debenedetti (FRDB) lists it on its data page.
- Since it ends in 2001, it won't show recent inequality trends. Its terms are unclear, so only pursue it if you have a personal contact.

## What you can do now
- **Today:** Register for the SIAB Campus File and build your cleaning pipeline and AKM code on it. Don't use it for any results you want to publish.
- **This week:**
  - Email the FDZ-IAB about the Regional File and the AKM effects.
  - Ask your advisor whether your department has a data-access contact or a Danish, German or Italian co-author. That is often what decides whether access happens in months or years.
  - Look for the next VisitINPS call.
- **Cross-country comparison:** Many papers using restricted data publish replication code and sometimes AKM effects or summary tables. These are good benchmarks, but they won't give you your own decomposition.

Evidence (what the judge was shown; for an image, a description of what was sent)
I found no dataset that is both open to download and suitable for a full AKM decomposition. The closest to "start now" is the Veneto Workers Histories, which you get by sending a signed form. The other options need institutional applications or in-person visits. I haven't checked costs, turnaround times, or eligibility for some of these, and I say so below.

## What you can start on now

**Veneto Workers Histories (VWH), Italy, 1975–2001**
- **What it is:** Social-security records for every private-sector firm in the provinces of Treviso and Vicenza, plus every worker those firms employed. Workers are followed across their whole careers, including jobs outside the area. There are three linkable files: a worker registry, yearly contribution records, and firm information with tax codes. The [FRDB data page](https://www.frdb.org/en/dati/dati-inps-carriere-lavorative-in-veneto/) lists it and the [FRDB description PDF](https://www.frdb.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/03/Description_database_VWH.pdf) documents it. [Jaime Arellano-Bover's page](https://www.jarellanobover.com/veneto-workers-histories-dataset-additional-resources) has extra resources for users.
- **Access:** Download the access form from FRDB, sign it, and email it to info@frdb.org. I could not find eligibility rules, fees, or turnaround time on the page. Ask FRDB before you plan around it.
- **Fit:** It has 27 years of data and stable worker and firm IDs. Card, Devicienti and Maida (2014) used it for rent-sharing work.
- **Limits:** The data end in 2001, so it can't speak to recent inequality trends. It also covers two provinces, not all of Italy.

**IAB's SIAB Scientific Use File, Germany**
- **What it is:** A 2% sample of German social-security records, 1975–2023, with a downloadable [Regional File](https://fdz.iab.de/en/pd_hd/factually-anonymous-version-of-the-sample-of-integrated-labour-market-biographies-siab-regionalfile-version-7523-v1/). Institutions apply for it through the [FDZ](https://fdz.iab.de/en/our-data-products/individual-and-household-data/siab/). I could not confirm eligibility for non-German institutions or the fees.
- **Why it doesn't work for AKM:** The Regional File has no shared establishment ID. It only has a counter that numbers establishments within each person's career. That means you can't build the worker–firm connected set. The [ZEW discussion paper](https://www.zew.de/fileadmin/FTP/dp/dp26025.pdf) and the [FDZ AKM documentation](https://doku.iab.de/fdz/reporte/2023/MR_01-23_EN.pdf) both point this way, but I am relying on search snippets, not the codebook. Check the codebook before you apply.
- **What it is good for:** Practice with the data structure and wage-inequality descriptives.

## What it takes to get real AKM-quality data

**Germany, full IAB data (LIAB, or SIAB weakly anonymous)**
- **Access:** On-site at an IAB research data centre, or remote access through the JoSuA system after first working on-site. You need an application and a data use agreement. See the [LIAB page](https://fdz.iab.de/en/int_bd_pd/linked-employer-employee-data-of-the-iab-liab-liab-longitudinal-model-1975-2021-version-1/) and the [FDZ SIAB page](https://fdz.iab.de/en/our-data-products/individual-and-household-data/siab/). Plan for a research stay in Nuremberg.
- **Precomputed AKM effects:** The FDZ offers worker and establishment effects estimated on the full data, covering 1985–2023 ([documentation](https://doku.iab.de/fdz/reporte/2025/MR_03-25_EN.pdf)). They are available only with the weakly anonymous data, through on-site or remote access, and may not combine with the SUF. They cover regular full-time workers only. This is the most practical route to a within- versus between-firm decomposition.

**Brazil, RAIS identified microdata**
- **Access:** You apply to the Ministry of Labor and Employment through your university. The application needs a project description and a justification for why you need identified data with consistent worker and employer IDs. It also needs a contact at your institution who can sign legal agreements. [Engbom and Moser's replication package](https://github.com/economoser/EM2022) describes this. The [Cambridge supplement](https://static.cambridge.org/content/id/urn:cambridge.org:id:article:S0007123425100859/resource/name/S0007123425100859sup001.pdf) confirms the university route. I found no processing-time estimate.
- **Public version:** The de-identified files are downloadable (the [`raisr` package](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/raisr/index.html) reads them). I did not verify whether they carry worker IDs you could follow over time. I would assume they don't until you check.
- **Fit:** It covers the whole formal sector over many years. Engbom and Moser's work on Brazilian wage inequality is close to your question.

**United States, LEHD**
- **Access:** Restricted microdata are available only inside a Federal Statistical Research Data Center. You need an approved project, and some files need extra IRS approval. See the [Census LEHD page](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/ces/data/restricted-use-data/lehd-data.html). Expect a long approval process.
- **Public alternative:** The public Job-to-Job Flows and Quarterly Workforce Indicators tables are aggregates, so you can't estimate AKM with them.

**Nordic countries**
- **Denmark:** Statistics Denmark authorises only Danish institutions. A foreign researcher needs a Danish affiliate ([overview](https://www.dst.dk/Site/Dst/SingleFiles/GetArchiveFile.aspx?fi=645846915&fo=0&ext=forskning)).
- **Norway:** Foreign institutions generally get only anonymous data. Identifiable data go through projects run by Norwegian institutions ([Statistics Norway guidelines](https://www.ssb.no/en/data-til-forskning)).
- **Sweden:** The MONA platform (Statistics Sweden's remote-access system) can't be used from the US or Canada ([terms of use](https://www.scb.se/en/services/ordering-data-and-statistics/microdata/mona--statistics-swedens-platform-for-access-to-microdata/rules-and-regulations/terms-of-use/)). Unless you are in the EU or EEA, you would need a local collaborator or a visit.

## My recommendation
1. Email FRDB this week for VWH, so you have something to build and test the estimation pipeline on.
2. Ask your advisor which of these they can sponsor or co-apply for. Germany needs a stay in Nuremberg, Brazil needs your university to sign legal agreements, and the Nordic routes need a local collaborator.
3. Use the [ABC of AKM guide](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.17034) for methods. It covers the limited-mobility bias that affects small samples like the SIAB, and your decomposition will need that correction.

## What I didn't verify
- Where you are based. That decides the Sweden and US options.
- Fees and turnaround for FRDB, IAB, and the Brazilian ministry.
- Whether other countries have workable options, such as Portugal, France, or Italy's national INPS data. I didn't search for them.

I can look into any of these next if you tell me where you are based.

Sources:

- [IAB AKM effects 1985–2023](https://doku.iab.de/fdz/reporte/2025/MR_03-25_EN.pdf)
- [IAB AKM effects (2023)](https://doku.iab.de/fdz/reporte/2023/MR_01-23_EN.pdf)
- [ZEW discussion paper](https://www.zew.de/fileadmin/FTP/dp/dp26025.pdf)
- [FRDB VWH page](https://www.frdb.org/en/dati/dati-inps-carriere-lavorative-in-veneto/)
- [FRDB VWH description](https://www.frdb.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/03/Description_database_VWH.pdf)
- [Arellano-Bover VWH resources](https://www.jarellanobover.com/veneto-workers-histories-dataset-additional-resources)
- [Engbom–Moser replication package](https://github.com/economoser/EM2022)
- [Cambridge data access supplement](https://static.cambridge.org/content/id/urn:cambridge.org:id:article:S0007123425100859/resource/name/S0007123425100859sup001.pdf)
- [raisr](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/raisr/index.html)
- [Census LEHD](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/ces/data/restricted-use-data/lehd-data.html)
- [Statistics Denmark](https://www.dst.dk/Site/Dst/SingleFiles/GetArchiveFile.aspx?fi=645846915&fo=0&ext=forskning)
- [Statistics Norway](https://www.ssb.no/en/data-til-forskning)
- [Statistics Sweden MONA terms](https://www.scb.se/en/services/ordering-data-and-statistics/microdata/mona--statistics-swedens-platform-for-access-to-microdata/rules-and-regulations/terms-of-use/)
- [The ABC of AKM](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.17034)

Evidence (what the judge was shown; for an image, a description of what was sent)
I found no dataset that is both open to download and suitable for a full AKM decomposition. The closest to "start now" is the Veneto Workers Histories, which you get by sending a signed form. The other options need institutional applications or in-person visits. I haven't checked costs, turnaround times, or eligibility for some of these, and I say so below.

## What you can start on now

**Veneto Workers Histories (VWH), Italy, 1975–2001**
- **What it is:** Social-security records for every private-sector firm in the provinces of Treviso and Vicenza, plus every worker those firms employed. Workers are followed across their whole careers, including jobs outside the area. There are three linkable files: a worker registry, yearly contribution records, and firm information with tax codes. The [FRDB data page](https://www.frdb.org/en/dati/dati-inps-carriere-lavorative-in-veneto/) lists it and the [FRDB description PDF](https://www.frdb.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/03/Description_database_VWH.pdf) documents it. [Jaime Arellano-Bover's page](https://www.jarellanobover.com/veneto-workers-histories-dataset-additional-resources) has extra resources for users.
- **Access:** Download the access form from FRDB, sign it, and email it to info@frdb.org. I could not find eligibility rules, fees, or turnaround time on the page. Ask FRDB before you plan around it.
- **Fit:** It has 27 years of data and stable worker and firm IDs. Card, Devicienti and Maida (2014) used it for rent-sharing work.
- **Limits:** The data end in 2001, so it can't speak to recent inequality trends. It also covers two provinces, not all of Italy.

**IAB's SIAB Scientific Use File, Germany**
- **What it is:** A 2% sample of German social-security records, 1975–2023, with a downloadable [Regional File](https://fdz.iab.de/en/pd_hd/factually-anonymous-version-of-the-sample-of-integrated-labour-market-biographies-siab-regionalfile-version-7523-v1/). Institutions apply for it through the [FDZ](https://fdz.iab.de/en/our-data-products/individual-and-household-data/siab/). I could not confirm eligibility for non-German institutions or the fees.
- **Why it doesn't work for AKM:** The Regional File has no shared establishment ID. It only has a counter that numbers establishments within each person's career. That means you can't build the worker–firm connected set. The [ZEW discussion paper](https://www.zew.de/fileadmin/FTP/dp/dp26025.pdf) and the [FDZ AKM documentation](https://doku.iab.de/fdz/reporte/2023/MR_01-23_EN.pdf) both point this way, but I am relying on search snippets, not the codebook. Check the codebook before you apply.
- **What it is good for:** Practice with the data structure and wage-inequality descriptives.

## What it takes to get real AKM-quality data

**Germany, full IAB data (LIAB, or SIAB weakly anonymous)**
- **Access:** On-site at an IAB research data centre, or remote access through the JoSuA system after first working on-site. You need an application and a data use agreement. See the [LIAB page](https://fdz.iab.de/en/int_bd_pd/linked-employer-employee-data-of-the-iab-liab-liab-longitudinal-model-1975-2021-version-1/) and the [FDZ SIAB page](https://fdz.iab.de/en/our-data-products/individual-and-household-data/siab/). Plan for a research stay in Nuremberg.
- **Precomputed AKM effects:** The FDZ offers worker and establishment effects estimated on the full data, covering 1985–2023 ([documentation](https://doku.iab.de/fdz/reporte/2025/MR_03-25_EN.pdf)). They are available only with the weakly anonymous data, through on-site or remote access, and may not combine with the SUF. They cover regular full-time workers only. This is the most practical route to a within- versus between-firm decomposition.

**Brazil, RAIS identified microdata**
- **Access:** You apply to the Ministry of Labor and Employment through your university. The application needs a project description and a justification for why you need identified data with consistent worker and employer IDs. It also needs a contact at your institution who can sign legal agreements. [Engbom and Moser's replication package](https://github.com/economoser/EM2022) describes this. The [Cambridge supplement](https://static.cambridge.org/content/id/urn:cambridge.org:id:article:S0007123425100859/resource/name/S0007123425100859sup001.pdf) confirms the university route. I found no processing-time estimate.
- **Public version:** The de-identified files are downloadable (the [`raisr` package](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/raisr/index.html) reads them). I did not verify whether they carry worker IDs you could follow over time. I would assume they don't until you check.
- **Fit:** It covers the whole formal sector over many years. Engbom and Moser's work on Brazilian wage inequality is close to your question.

**United States, LEHD**
- **Access:** Restricted microdata are available only inside a Federal Statistical Research Data Center. You need an approved project, and some files need extra IRS approval. See the [Census LEHD page](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/ces/data/restricted-use-data/lehd-data.html). Expect a long approval process.
- **Public alternative:** The public Job-to-Job Flows and Quarterly Workforce Indicators tables are aggregates, so you can't estimate AKM with them.

**Nordic countries**
- **Denmark:** Statistics Denmark authorises only Danish institutions. A foreign researcher needs a Danish affiliate ([overview](https://www.dst.dk/Site/Dst/SingleFiles/GetArchiveFile.aspx?fi=645846915&fo=0&ext=forskning)).
- **Norway:** Foreign institutions generally get only anonymous data. Identifiable data go through projects run by Norwegian institutions ([Statistics Norway guidelines](https://www.ssb.no/en/data-til-forskning)).
- **Sweden:** The MONA platform (Statistics Sweden's remote-access system) can't be used from the US or Canada ([terms of use](https://www.scb.se/en/services/ordering-data-and-statistics/microdata/mona--statistics-swedens-platform-for-access-to-microdata/rules-and-regulations/terms-of-use/)). Unless you are in the EU or EEA, you would need a local collaborator or a visit.

## My recommendation
1. Email FRDB this week for VWH, so you have something to build and test the estimation pipeline on.
2. Ask your advisor which of these they can sponsor or co-apply for. Germany needs a stay in Nuremberg, Brazil needs your university to sign legal agreements, and the Nordic routes need a local collaborator.
3. Use the [ABC of AKM guide](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.17034) for methods. It covers the limited-mobility bias that affects small samples like the SIAB, and your decomposition will need that correction.

## What I didn't verify
- Where you are based. That decides the Sweden and US options.
- Fees and turnaround for FRDB, IAB, and the Brazilian ministry.
- Whether other countries have workable options, such as Portugal, France, or Italy's national INPS data. I didn't search for them.

I can look into any of these next if you tell me where you are based.

2. Ask your advisor which of these they can sponsor or co-apply for. Germany needs a stay in Nuremberg, Brazil needs your university to sign legal agreements, and the Nordic routes need a local collaborator.
3. Use the [ABC of AKM guide](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.17034) for methods. It covers the limited-mobility bias that affects small samples like the SIAB, and your decomposition will need that correction.

- Where you are based. That decides the Sweden and US options.
- Fees and turnaround for FRDB, IAB, and the Brazilian ministry.
- Whether other countries have workable options, such as Portugal, France, or Italy's national INPS data. I didn't search for them.

I found no dataset that is both open to download and suitable for a full AKM decomposition. The closest to "start now" is the Veneto Workers Histories, which you get by sending a signed form. The other options need institutional applications or in-person visits. I haven't checked costs, turnaround times, or eligibility for some of these, and I say so below.

## What you can start on now

**Veneto Workers Histories (VWH), Italy, 1975–2001**
- **What it is:** Social-security records for every private-sector firm in the provinces of Treviso and Vicenza, plus every worker those firms employed. Workers are followed across their whole careers, including jobs outside the area. There are three linkable files: a worker registry, yearly contribution records, and firm information with tax codes. The [FRDB data page](https://www.frdb.org/en/dati/dati-inps-carriere-lavorative-in-veneto/) lists it and the [FRDB description PDF](https://www.frdb.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/03/Description_database_VWH.pdf) documents it. [Jaime Arellano-Bover's page](https://www.jarellanobover.com/veneto-workers-histories-dataset-additional-resources) has extra resources for users.
- **Access:** Download the access form from FRDB, sign it, and email it to info@frdb.org. I could not find eligibility rules, fees, or turnaround time on the page. Ask FRDB before you plan around it.
- **Fit:** It has 27 years of data and stable worker and firm IDs. Card, Devicienti and Maida (2014) used it for rent-sharing work.
- **Limits:** The data end in 2001, so it can't speak to recent inequality trends. It also covers two provinces, not all of Italy.

**IAB's SIAB Scientific Use File, Germany**
- **What it is:** A 2% sample of German social-security records, 1975–2023, with a downloadable [Regional File](https://fdz.iab.de/en/pd_hd/factually-anonymous-version-of-the-sample-of-integrated-labour-market-biographies-siab-regionalfile-version-7523-v1/). Institutions apply for it through the [FDZ](https://fdz.iab.de/en/our-data-products/individual-and-household-data/siab/). I could not confirm eligibility for non-German institutions or the fees.
- **Why it doesn't work for AKM:** The Regional File has no shared establishment ID. It only has a counter that numbers establishments within each person's career. That means you can't build the worker–firm connected set. The [ZEW discussion paper](https://www.zew.de/fileadmin/FTP/dp/dp26025.pdf) and the [FDZ AKM documentation](https://doku.iab.de/fdz/reporte/2023/MR_01-23_EN.pdf) both point this way, but I am relying on search snippets, not the codebook. Check the codebook before you apply.
- **What it is good for:** Practice with the data structure and wage-inequality descriptives.

## What it takes to get real AKM-quality data

**Germany, full IAB data (LIAB, or SIAB weakly anonymous)**
- **Access:** On-site at an IAB research data centre, or remote access through the JoSuA system after first working on-site. You need an application and a data use agreement. See the [LIAB page](https://fdz.iab.de/en/int_bd_pd/linked-employer-employee-data-of-the-iab-liab-liab-longitudinal-model-1975-2021-version-1/) and the [FDZ SIAB page](https://fdz.iab.de/en/our-data-products/individual-and-household-data/siab/). Plan for a research stay in Nuremberg.
- **Precomputed AKM effects:** The FDZ offers worker and establishment effects estimated on the full data, covering 1985–2023 ([documentation](https://doku.iab.de/fdz/reporte/2025/MR_03-25_EN.pdf)). They are available only with the weakly anonymous data, through on-site or remote access, and may not combine with the SUF. They cover regular full-time workers only. This is the most practical route to a within- versus between-firm decomposition.

**Brazil, RAIS identified microdata**
- **Access:** You apply to the Ministry of Labor and Employment through your university. The application needs a project description and a justification for why you need identified data with consistent worker and employer IDs. It also needs a contact at your institution who can sign legal agreements. [Engbom and Moser's replication package](https://github.com/economoser/EM2022) describes this. The [Cambridge supplement](https://static.cambridge.org/content/id/urn:cambridge.org:id:article:S0007123425100859/resource/name/S0007123425100859sup001.pdf) confirms the university route. I found no processing-time estimate.
- **Public version:** The de-identified files are downloadable (the [`raisr` package](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/raisr/index.html) reads them). I did not verify whether they carry worker IDs you could follow over time. I would assume they don't until you check.
- **Fit:** It covers the whole formal sector over many years. Engbom and Moser's work on Brazilian wage inequality is close to your question.

**United States, LEHD**
- **Access:** Restricted microdata are available only inside a Federal Statistical Research Data Center. You need an approved project, and some files need extra IRS approval. See the [Census LEHD page](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/ces/data/restricted-use-data/lehd-data.html). Expect a long approval process.
- **Public alternative:** The public Job-to-Job Flows and Quarterly Workforce Indicators tables are aggregates, so you can't estimate AKM with them.

**Nordic countries**
- **Denmark:** Statistics Denmark authorises only Danish institutions. A foreign researcher needs a Danish affiliate ([overview](https://www.dst.dk/Site/Dst/SingleFiles/GetArchiveFile.aspx?fi=645846915&fo=0&ext=forskning)).
- **Norway:** Foreign institutions generally get only anonymous data. Identifiable data go through projects run by Norwegian institutions ([Statistics Norway guidelines](https://www.ssb.no/en/data-til-forskning)).
- **Sweden:** The MONA platform (Statistics Sweden's remote-access system) can't be used from the US or Canada ([terms of use](https://www.scb.se/en/services/ordering-data-and-statistics/microdata/mona--statistics-swedens-platform-for-access-to-microdata/rules-and-regulations/terms-of-use/)). Unless you are in the EU or EEA, you would need a local collaborator or a visit.

## My recommendation
1. Email FRDB this week for VWH, so you have something to build and test the estimation pipeline on.
2. Ask your advisor which of these they can sponsor or co-apply for. Germany needs a stay in Nuremberg, Brazil needs your university to sign legal agreements, and the Nordic routes need a local collaborator.
3. Use the [ABC of AKM guide](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.17034) for methods. It covers the limited-mobility bias that affects small samples like the SIAB, and your decomposition will need that correction.

## What I didn't verify

- Fees and turnaround for FRDB, IAB, and the Brazilian ministry.
- Whether other countries have workable options, such as Portugal, France, or Italy's national INPS data. I didn't search for them.

Evidence (what the judge was shown; for an image, a description of what was sent)
Short version: I found one dataset you can request today (Veneto, Italy), but it only covers part of Italy and stops in 2001. The other options are restricted, and the pages I checked didn't give me eligibility rules, fees or timelines.

## Start now

**Veneto Workers Histories (VWH), Italy**
- **What it is:** INPS social-security records, 1975–2001, with linked person, firm and contract files. This is the structure AKM needs, and the FRDB notes that it's commonly used for that.
- **Coverage caveat:** The FRDB page says the data cover all private-sector firms in the provinces of Treviso and Vicenza and every worker those firms employed. Other sources describe it more broadly as workers who ever worked in Veneto. Read the [data description PDF](https://www.frdb.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/03/Description_database_VWH.pdf) before you rely on it. Agriculture and public administration are excluded.
- **Access:** You fill in and sign a form on the [FRDB page](https://www.frdb.org/en/dati/dati-inps-carriere-lavorative-in-veneto/) and email it to info@frdb.org. You must cite Università Ca' Foscari Venezia and Giuseppe Tattara as the source. I didn't find eligibility conditions or a turnaround time, so ask them. [Arellano-Bover's page](https://www.jarellanobover.com/veneto-workers-histories-dataset-additional-resources) has extra notes for users.
- **Fit for your question:** It spans 27 years, so it fits a ten-year panel. But it's one region, and it ends in 2001, so it can't speak to recent inequality trends. It's best for learning the method and building a pipeline, or for a first-year paper.

**Teaching and test files**
- The IAB Campus File (SIAB CF 7508) is free after registering, but it's for teaching only. It's a 20% sample of one cohort of unemployment-benefit entrants, and it has no establishment ID, so it can't support AKM.
- The IAB also posts [random test data](https://fdz.iab.de/en/int_bd_pd/linked-employer-employee-data-of-the-iab-liab-liab-longitudinal-model-1975-2021-version-1/) for the LIAB. It's meant for writing and debugging code and isn't suitable for analysis.

**Public tabulations**
- The Census [Job-to-Job Flows](https://lehd.ces.census.gov/data/j2j_subsector_research.html) tables are public but aggregate. They are useful for context, not for AKM.

## Restricted options, ranked by realism

1. **Germany: IAB LIAB** (linked employer-employee data, longitudinal model 1975–2024 is the newest version I saw).
   - **Access:** On-site use at the research data centre in Nuremberg, which includes remote access after you've used it on-site. The [FDZ page](https://fdz.iab.de/en/int_bd_pd/linked-employer-employee-data-of-the-iab-liab-liab-longitudinal-model-1975-2021-version-1/) notes that person and establishment AKM effects are available on request.
   - **Gaps:** There is no scientific use file for LIAB, and the establishment sample comes from a stratified survey panel. The page didn't state the fees, eligibility or application steps. Start with [fdz.iab.de/en/data-access](https://fdz.iab.de/en/data-access) and iab.fdz@iab.de.
   - **Also:** The full SIAB (a 2% sample of individual employment histories) has the establishment ID, but only the on-site version. The public SIAB-Regionalfile doesn't have it. The guides I found describe on-site use in Nuremberg or at partner sites in Germany, France, Luxembourg, Poland and Spain, plus an application and a contract.

2. **US: LEHD through a Federal Statistical Research Data Center (FSRDC).**
   - **Access:** You need an approved project, and some files need extra IRS approval because they contain federal tax information. Only a subset of states is available, and the data generally run from 2000. See the [Census page](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/ces/data/restricted-use-data/lehd-data.html). Expect a long approval process.
   - **Gap:** LEHD records quarterly earnings, so you don't observe wages directly.

3. **Brazil: identified RAIS.**
   - **Access:** It's not public. You request it from the Ministry of Labour through the gov.br service "Solicitar acesso aos dados identificados RAIS e CAGED", and sign a confidentiality agreement. I couldn't confirm the exact requirements or timing. See the [PDET microdata page](https://www.gov.br/trabalho-e-emprego/pt-br/acesso-a-informacao/acoes-e-programas/programas-projetos-acoes-obras-e-atividades/estatisticas-trabalho/microdados-rais-e-caged-e-caged) and the [service link](https://www.gov.br/pt-br/servicos/solicitar-acesso-aos-dados-identificados-rais-e-caged). This is plausibly the most accessible option for a foreign researcher, but I haven't verified that.
   - **Gap:** I didn't check whether the public, non-identified RAIS files can link workers across years, so don't assume they can.

4. **Denmark: IDA.**
   - **Access:** The sources I found are old (about 2010–2011). They say access goes to permanent research environments, and foreign researchers generally need a tie to a Danish institution. Short version: I found one dataset you can request today (Veneto, Italy), but it only covers part of Italy and stops in 2001. The other options are restricted, and the pages I checked didn't give me eligibility rules, fees or timelines.

## Start now

**Veneto Workers Histories (VWH), Italy**
- **What it is:** INPS social-security records, 1975–2001, with linked person, firm and contract files. This is the structure AKM needs, and the FRDB notes that it's commonly used for that.
- **Coverage caveat:** The FRDB page says the data cover all private-sector firms in the provinces of Treviso and Vicenza and every worker those firms employed. Other sources describe it more broadly as workers who ever worked in Veneto. Read the [data description PDF](https://www.frdb.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/03/Description_database_VWH.pdf) before you rely on it. Agriculture and public administration are excluded.
- **Access:** You fill in and sign a form on the [FRDB page](https://www.frdb.org/en/dati/dati-inps-carriere-lavorative-in-veneto/) and email it to info@frdb.org. You must cite Università Ca' Foscari Venezia and Giuseppe Tattara as the source. I didn't find eligibility conditions or a turnaround time, so ask them. [Arellano-Bover's page](https://www.jarellanobover.com/veneto-workers-histories-dataset-additional-resources) has extra notes for users.
- **Fit for your question:** It spans 27 years, so it fits a ten-year panel. But it's one region, and it ends in 2001, so it can't speak to recent inequality trends. It's best for learning the method and building a pipeline, or for a first-year paper.

**Teaching and test files**
- The IAB Campus File (SIAB CF 7508) is free after registering, but it's for teaching only. It's a 20% sample of one cohort of unemployment-benefit entrants, and it has no establishment ID, so it can't support AKM.
- The IAB also posts [random test data](https://fdz.iab.de/en/int_bd_pd/linked-employer-employee-data-of-the-iab-liab-liab-longitudinal-model-1975-2021-version-1/) for the LIAB. It's meant for writing and debugging code and isn't suitable for analysis.

**Public tabulations**
- The Census [Job-to-Job Flows](https://lehd.ces.census.gov/data/j2j_subsector_research.html) tables are public but aggregate. They are useful for context, not for AKM.

## Restricted options, ranked by realism

1. **Germany: IAB LIAB** (linked employer-employee data, longitudinal model 1975–2024 is the newest version I saw).
   - **Access:** On-site use at the research data centre in Nuremberg, which includes remote access after you've used it on-site. The [FDZ page](https://fdz.iab.de/en/int_bd_pd/linked-employer-employee-data-of-the-iab-liab-liab-longitudinal-model-1975-2021-version-1/) notes that person and establishment AKM effects are available on request.
   - **Gaps:** There is no scientific use file for LIAB, and the establishment sample comes from a stratified survey panel. The page didn't state the fees, eligibility or application steps. Start with [fdz.iab.de/en/data-access](https://fdz.iab.de/en/data-access) and iab.fdz@iab.de.
   - **Also:** The full SIAB (a 2% sample of individual employment histories) has the establishment ID, but only the on-site version. The public SIAB-Regionalfile doesn't have it. The guides I found describe on-site use in Nuremberg or at partner sites in Germany, France, Luxembourg, Poland and Spain, plus an application and a contract.

2. **US: LEHD through a Federal Statistical Research Data Center (FSRDC).**
   - **Access:** You need an approved project, and some files need extra IRS approval because they contain federal tax information. Only a subset of states is available, and the data generally run from 2000. See the [Census page](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/ces/data/restricted-use-data/lehd-data.html). Expect a long approval process.
   - **Gap:** LEHD records quarterly earnings, so you don't observe wages directly.

3. **Brazil: identified RAIS.**
   - **Access:** It's not public. You request it from the Ministry of Labour through the gov.br service "Solicitar acesso aos dados identificados RAIS e CAGED", and sign a confidentiality agreement. I couldn't confirm the exact requirements or timing. See the [PDET microdata page](https://www.gov.br/trabalho-e-emprego/pt-br/acesso-a-informacao/acoes-e-programas/programas-projetos-acoes-obras-e-atividades/estatisticas-trabalho/microdados-rais-e-caged-e-caged) and the [service link](https://www.gov.br/pt-br/servicos/solicitar-acesso-aos-dados-identificados-rais-e-caged). This is plausibly the most accessible option for a foreign researcher, but I haven't verified that.
   - **Gap:** I didn't check whether the public, non-identified RAIS files can link workers across years, so don't assume they can.

4. **Denmark: IDA.**
   - **Access:** The sources I found are old (about 2010–2011). They say access goes to permanent research environments, and foreign researchers generally need a tie to a Danish institution. Remote access exists. See [this IDA description](https://wp.druid.dk/wp/20100016.pdf). Check Statistics Denmark's current rules, since this may have changed.

5. **Portugal (Quadros de Pessoal), Norway, Sweden.** Papers use these data, but my searches found nothing on access. I'm not recommending them, and I couldn't verify that any fixed-effects estimates are publicly posted for these or any other country.

Only a subset of states is available, and the data generally run from 2000. See the [Census page](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/ces/data/restricted-use-data/lehd-data.html). Expect a long approval process.
   - **Gap:** LEHD records quarterly earnings, so you don't observe wages directly.

3. **Brazil: identified RAIS.**
   - **Access:** It's not public. You request it from the Ministry of Labour through the gov.br service "Solicitar acesso aos dados identificados RAIS e CAGED", and sign a confidentiality agreement. I couldn't confirm the exact requirements or timing. See the [PDET microdata page](https://www.gov.br/trabalho-e-emprego/pt-br/acesso-a-informacao/acoes-e-programas/programas-projetos-acoes-obras-e-atividades/estatisticas-trabalho/microdados-rais-e-caged-e-caged) and the [service link](https://www.gov.br/pt-br/servicos/solicitar-acesso-aos-dados-identificados-rais-e-caged). This is plausibly the most accessible option for a foreign researcher, but I haven't verified that.
   - **Gap:** I didn't check whether the public, non-identified RAIS files can link workers across years, so don't assume they can.

4. **Denmark: IDA.**
   - **Access:** The sources I found are old (about 2010–2011). They say access goes to permanent research environments, and foreign researchers generally need a tie to a Danish institution. Remote access exists. See [this IDA description](https://wp.druid.dk/wp/20100016.pdf). Check Statistics Denmark's current rules, since this may have changed.

5. **Portugal (Quadros de Pessoal), Norway, Sweden.** Papers use these data, but my searches found nothing on access. I'm not recommending them, and I couldn't verify that any fixed-effects estimates are publicly posted for these or any other country.

Prompt

I'm a second-year PhD student in labor economics. I want to decompose the rise in wage inequality into within-firm and between-firm parts with an AKM-style model (worker and firm fixed effects), so I need linked employer-employee microdata where I can follow individual workers as they move between employers over at least ten years. Any country is fine. I already know most data like this is restricted, so please be honest about what it would actually take to get access to each option, and tell me if there is anything I could start working with right away.

Please search the web rather than answering from memory, and check that each dataset you recommend really exists and how it can be accessed.

Graders — what "good" means for this case
01-recall-german-iabllm

PASS if the final answer recommends or lists German linked employer-employee data from the Institute for Employment Research (IAB) and its Research Data Centre (FDZ der BA im IAB) as a candidate, in any version: for example the Linked Employer-Employee Data of the IAB (LIAB, including the LIAB longitudinal model), the Sample of Integrated Labour Market Biographies (SIAB) linked to establishment data, the Integrated Employment Biographies (IEB), the Employment History (BeH) or the Establishment History Panel (BHP) combined with worker records. FAIL if the answer does not mention any German IAB/FDZ worker-establishment data, or mentions it only to say it is unsuitable.

02-recall-us-lehdllm

PASS if the final answer recommends or lists the confidential microdata of the US Census Bureau's Longitudinal Employer-Household Dynamics program (LEHD, also called the LEHD microdata, LEHD infrastructure files or LEHD Snapshot, built from state unemployment-insurance wage records) as a candidate source of linked employer-employee data. FAIL if the answer does not mention LEHD microdata, mentions only the public LEHD tabulations (QWI, LODES, J2J or OnTheMap) without the restricted worker-level microdata, or mentions LEHD only to say it is unsuitable.

03-recall-brazil-raisllm

PASS if the final answer recommends or lists Brazil's RAIS (Relação Anual de Informações Sociais, the Annual Social Information Report administered by the Brazilian Ministry of Labour and Employment) as a candidate source of linked employer-employee data, in any version. FAIL if the answer does not mention RAIS, or mentions it only to say it is unsuitable.

04-access-german-fdz-applicationllm

PASS if the final answer mentions German IAB linked employer-employee data (LIAB, SIAB, IEB or other IAB/FDZ data) and states that getting it requires applying to the IAB Research Data Centre (FDZ) with a research project and concluding a use agreement or contract, or states that the data can be analysed only through on-site use at an FDZ location, remote desktop access or remote execution (submitting code) rather than being downloaded freely. FAIL if the answer does not mention the German IAB/FDZ data, gives no information about how it is accessed, or states that it can be downloaded freely without an application or contract.

05-access-us-fsrdc-projectllm

PASS if the final answer mentions the US Census Bureau's LEHD microdata and states that access requires an approved research project or proposal and takes place inside a secure Federal Statistical Research Data Center (FSRDC, also called a Census Research Data Center or RDC), for example also mentioning Special Sworn Status or additional IRS/SSA approval. Stating either the approved-project requirement or the FSRDC-only access is enough. FAIL if the answer does not mention LEHD microdata, gives no information about how they are accessed, or states that the worker-level LEHD microdata can be downloaded publicly.

06-access-brazil-ministry-agreementllm

PASS if the final answer mentions Brazil's RAIS and states that the identified version (with the worker and firm identifiers needed to follow individuals across employers) is restricted and is obtained through a formal request to, and agreement with, the Brazilian Ministry of Labour and Employment (for example a technical cooperation agreement, data-use agreement or similar approval), as opposed to the de-identified public files. FAIL if the answer does not mention RAIS, gives no information about how identified RAIS is accessed, or states that RAIS with worker identifiers can be freely downloaded without any agreement or approval.

07-trap-lehd-public-tablesllm

PASS if the final answer does not present the public LEHD data products (LEHD Origin-Destination Employment Statistics, LODES; Quarterly Workforce Indicators, QWI; Job-to-Job Flows, J2J; Post-Secondary Employment Outcomes, PSEO; or the OnTheMap tool) as worker-level linked employer-employee microdata in which individual workers can be followed across employers or used to estimate worker and firm fixed effects. Not mentioning them passes; mentioning them while noting that they are aggregated public tabulations (for example at census-block, county or industry level) and not individual-level microdata also passes. FAIL if the answer recommends any of these public tables as a dataset that lets the user track individual workers across firms or estimate an AKM model.

08-long-tailllm

PASS if the final answer recommends or lists at least one of these less known linked employer-employee datasets as a candidate: (a) the Canadian Employer-Employee Dynamics Database (CEEDD) of Statistics Canada; (b) the Finnish Longitudinal Employer-Employee Data (FLEED) of Statistics Finland; (c) the Austrian Social Security Database (ASSD). FAIL if the answer mentions none of them as a candidate.

## Recommendation

For a commercial product, start with **AMI**, then add **NOTSOFAR-1** and **DiPCo**. Skip ICSI unless you're prepared to confirm its licence with Edinburgh or LDC.

Every licence below is the dataset owner's published statement. I haven't had a lawyer read them, so have someone do that before you ship.

### 1. AMI Meeting Corpus: the core set
- **What it is:** about 100 hours of real English meetings. They include scenario meetings, where participants play assigned roles, and natural ones. Audio comes from individual headsets and lapel mics, plus two table-top microphone arrays (8 channels each).
- **Licence:** CC BY 4.0, which allows commercial use with attribution. The [licence page](https://groups.inf.ed.ac.uk/ami/corpus/license.shtml) says "The AMI corpus and its annotations" are CC BY 4.0. The [download page](https://groups.inf.ed.ac.uk/ami/download/) says both annotation zips were relicensed to CC BY 4.0 in April 2017. Other pages still say "some annotations", so I couldn't fully close that gap.
- **Access:** free. You pick meetings and streams on the [download page](https://groups.inf.ed.ac.uk/ami/download/). The array audio is about 360 MB per meeting. It is also mirrored on [OpenSLR (SLR16)](https://www.openslr.org/resources.php), but OpenSLR's page states no licence, so use the Edinburgh licence.
- **Caveats:**
  - Annotations are in NXT format, and the download page doesn't spell out diarization or word timing. Check the annotation documentation for speaker segments before relying on them. Existing AMI RTTM files used in diarization toolkits are derived from these annotations.
  - Treat Hugging Face mirrors with caution. One lists AMI as "non-commercial", which contradicts Edinburgh's licence.
  - Many scenario meetings are role-played, so the content is less spontaneous than real business meetings.

### 2. NOTSOFAR-1 (Microsoft): real far-field meetings
- **What it is:** [recorded meetings](https://github.com/microsoft/NOTSOFAR1-Challenge), 237 of them at about 6 minutes each. That's roughly 24 hours, by my own estimate. They were recorded in 30 conference rooms with 4–8 attendees and 35 unique speakers, on both multi-channel array devices and single-channel devices. The ~1,000 hours of simulated training data in the same release is synthetic, so leave it out given your real-recordings requirement.
- **Licence:** CC BY 4.0, per the repo.
- **Access:** free. Create a Hugging Face token, set `HF_TOKEN`, and use the download helpers in `utils/notsofar_dataset.py`.
- **Caveat:** the page doesn't describe the speaker-turn annotation format. It says ground truth is available for the eval sets and that transcript upgrades are underway for train and dev. Check the annotation coverage per split before you plan around it.

### 3. DiPCo (Amazon): small but properly far-field
- **What it is:** [10 dinner-party sessions](https://zenodo.org/records/8122551) of 15–45 minutes each, with 4 speakers in English. Each speaker has a close-talk mic, and five 7-mic far-field array devices record the room.
- **Licence:** CDLA-Permissive 1.0, which permits commercial use.
- **Access:** open download of a 13.4 GB archive from Zenodo, no login needed.
- **Caveat:** it is casual dinner conversation, not business meetings, and it's small. It is useful as extra far-field data.

### Not recommended, or unresolved
- **ICSI Meeting Corpus:** real research-group meetings with headset and tabletop mics. The licensing is unclear.
  - LDC distributes it under its own agreement, and LDC fees apply for non-members.
  - A Hugging Face card says Edinburgh redistributes it under CC BY 4.0. The [Edinburgh ICSI page](https://groups.inf.ed.ac.uk/ami/icsi/) does say signals, transcription and some annotations are CC BY 4.0.
  - I couldn't find a diarization annotation listed there. The Whipscribe page's claim that it's on OpenSLR as SLR106 is wrong. SLR106 is a West African speech corpus.
  - Write to Edinburgh or LDC to confirm before using it.
- **CHiME-6:** real English dinner parties with far-field arrays, but it is CC BY-SA 4.0. ShareAlike may not fit a commercial model, so ask a lawyer before using it.
- **AliMeeting and AISHELL-4:** Mandarin, and CC BY-SA 4.0, so they fail both of your constraints.
- **Paid vendor data:** The Agentic Data Company sells multi-party English conversations under a commercial licence. The audio isn't recorded on a far-field array. It is mixed down or convolved with a room response to simulate far-field, so it conflicts with your "not simulated" requirement. I didn't verify the vendor beyond its listing.

### Next steps
1. Pull AMI array audio and annotations. Confirm you can derive speaker turns from the annotations.
2. Pull the NOTSOFAR-1 recorded dev/eval sets and check the annotation format.
3. Keep a record of each licence and attribution requirement. CC BY needs credit, and the AMI page also says no endorsement may be implied.
4. If you need more business-style meeting data, you may need to commission recordings or buy a licence from a vendor that records real meetings. I didn't find a public dataset that does this.

Sources:
- [AMI licence](https://groups.inf.ed.ac.uk/ami/corpus/license.shtml)
- [AMI download](https://groups.inf.ed.ac.uk/ami/download/)
- [AMI and ICSI Corpora](https://groups.inf.ed.ac.uk/ami/)
- [ICSI at Edinburgh](https://groups.inf.ed.ac.uk/ami/icsi/)
- [NOTSOFAR-1 repo](https://github.com/microsoft/NOTSOFAR1-Challenge)
- [DiPCo on Zenodo](https://zenodo.org/records/8122551)
- [OpenSLR resources](https://www.openslr.org/resources.php)
- [LDC ICSI transcripts](https://catalog.ldc.upenn.edu/LDC2004T04)
- [Spirelight meeting dataset comparison](https://www.spirelight.ai/guides/meeting-speech-datasets)
- [DiariZen licence issue](https://github.com/BUTSpeechFIT/DiariZen/issues/32)
- [The Agentic Data Company](https://theagenticdatacompany.com/datasets/multi-party-conversations)

  - Annotations are in NXT format, and the download page doesn't spell out diarization or word timing. Check the annotation documentation for speaker segments before relying on them. Existing AMI RTTM files used in diarization toolkits are derived from these annotations.
  - Treat Hugging Face mirrors with caution. One lists AMI as "non-commercial", which contradicts Edinburgh's licence.
  - Many scenario meetings are role-played, so the content is less spontaneous than real business meetings.

### 2. NOTSOFAR-1 (Microsoft): real far-field meetings
- **What it is:** [recorded meetings](https://github.com/microsoft/NOTSOFAR1-Challenge), 237 of them at about 6 minutes each. That's roughly 24 hours, by my own estimate. They were recorded in 30 conference rooms with 4–8 attendees and 35 unique speakers, on both multi-channel array devices and single-channel devices. The ~1,000 hours of simulated training data in the same release is synthetic, so leave it out given your real-recordings requirement.
- **Licence:** CC BY 4.0, per the repo.
- **Access:** free. Create a Hugging Face token, set `HF_TOKEN`, and use the download helpers in `utils/notsofar_dataset.py`.
- **Caveat:** the page doesn't describe the speaker-turn annotation format. It says ground truth is available for the eval sets and that transcript upgrades are underway for train and dev. Check the annotation coverage per split before you plan around it.

### 3. DiPCo (Amazon): small but properly far-field
- **What it is:** [10 dinner-party sessions](https://zenodo.org/records/8122551) of 15–45 minutes each, with 4 speakers in English. Each speaker has a close-talk mic, and five 7-mic far-field array devices record the room.
- **Licence:** CDLA-Permissive 1.0, which permits commercial use.
- **Access:** open download of a 13.4 GB archive from Zenodo, no login needed.
- **Caveat:** it is casual dinner conversation, not business meetings, and it's small. It is useful as extra far-field data.

### Not recommended, or unresolved
- **ICSI Meeting Corpus:** real research-group meetings with headset and tabletop mics. The licensing is unclear.
  - LDC distributes it under its own agreement, and LDC fees apply for non-members.
  - A Hugging Face card says Edinburgh redistributes it under CC BY 4.0. The [Edinburgh ICSI page](https://groups.inf.ed.ac.uk/ami/icsi/) does say signals, transcription and some annotations are CC BY 4.0.
  - I couldn't find a diarization annotation listed there. The Whipscribe page's claim that it's on OpenSLR as SLR106 is wrong. SLR106 is a West African speech corpus.
  - Write to Edinburgh or LDC to confirm before using it.
- **CHiME-6:** real English dinner parties with far-field arrays, but it is CC BY-SA 4.0. ShareAlike may not fit a commercial model, so ask a lawyer before using it.
- **AliMeeting and AISHELL-4:** Mandarin, and CC BY-SA 4.0, so they fail both of your constraints.
- **Paid vendor data:** The Agentic Data Company sells multi-party English conversations under a commercial licence. The audio isn't recorded on a far-field array. It is mixed down or convolved with a room response to simulate far-field, so it conflicts with your "not simulated" requirement. I didn't verify the vendor beyond its listing.

### Next steps
1. Pull AMI array audio and annotations. Confirm you can derive speaker turns from the annotations.
2. Pull the NOTSOFAR-1 recorded dev/eval sets and check the annotation format.
3. Keep a record of each licence and attribution requirement. CC BY needs credit, and the AMI page also says no endorsement may be implied.
4. If you need more business-style meeting data, you may need to commission recordings or buy a licence from a vendor that records real meetings. I didn't find a public dataset that does this.

Evidence (what the judge was shown; for an image, a description of what was sent)
**Recommendation: use AMI as your core dataset. Add DiPCo and CHiME-6 only as secondary sets for far-field robustness. There's no other free English meeting corpus that fits all your criteria.**

## 1. AMI Meeting Corpus (primary)
- **What it is:** About 100 hours of real, non-simulated meetings in English. Roughly two-thirds are scenario-driven, where participants play assigned roles, so they're staged but spoken naturally. The rest are natural meetings. It's the closest match to business-style meetings I found.
- **Audio:** Individual headsets, lapel mics, and a headset mix. The far-field audio comes from two table-top microphone arrays. The official download page lists it as "audio channels from two table-top arrays".
- **Licence:** The [AMI licence page](https://groups.inf.ed.ac.uk/ami/corpus/license.shtml) states that the corpus and its annotations are CC BY 4.0. That licence allows commercial use if you give attribution. The [download page](https://groups.inf.ed.ac.uk/ami/download/) says the manual (v1.6.2) and automatic (v1.5.1) annotation zips were also changed to CC BY 4.0. It adds that some other annotations may not be covered, so check the files you actually use.
- **Access:** Free download from the [AMI download page](https://groups.inf.ed.ac.uk/ami/download/). You pick meetings and audio streams there, and the annotations come as NXT-format zips. I didn't confirm which annotation file carries the speaker segmentation. The [annotation docs](https://groups.inf.ed.ac.uk/ami/corpus/annotation.shtml) should say.
- **Caveats:**
  - A Hugging Face card for `knkarthick/AMI` says "non-commercial". That contradicts the official CC BY 4.0 licence and looks like an error. Rely on the Edinburgh pages and keep a copy of the licence text.
  - Most speakers are non-native English speakers. The recordings are also from 2000s-era rooms, so they're a limited sample of modern conference-call audio.
  - Licences on pretrained models still matter. A pyannote or DiariZen checkpoint trained on mixed data can carry restrictions even though AMI itself is clean.

## 2. DiPCo (secondary, far-field)
- **What it is:** Dinner-party conversations, not meetings. It has 10 sessions of 15–45 minutes, with four people per session. Each person wore a close-talk mic. Five far-field devices with 7-mic arrays were placed around the room.
- **Licence:** CDLA-Permissive 1.0, which allows commercial use. The [Zenodo record](https://zenodo.org/records/8122551), the Interspeech paper and Amazon's release blog all agree.
- **Access:** Free from Zenodo (about 12 GB). The original S3 link has expired.
- **Caveat:** It's small, and the content is casual dinner talk.

## 3. CHiME-6 (secondary, far-field)
- **What it is:** English dinner-party recordings. It has 4 participants per session, recorded on several distant 4-mic Kinect arrays.
- **Licence:** CC BY-SA 4.0, listed on [OpenSLR SLR150](https://www.openslr.org/150/). That allows commercial use, but ShareAlike applies to derivatives. Have a lawyer decide whether your trained models count as derivatives before you use it for a commercial product.
- **Access:** Free from OpenSLR. Training data is about 97 GB, and the JSON transcriptions are a separate file.
- **Caveat:** Its content is domestic and very hard acoustically. It's useful for robustness, but it isn't meeting-like.

## Ruled out or not usable as-is
- **ICSI Meeting Corpus:** The Edinburgh [ICSI page](https://groups.inf.ed.ac.uk/ami/icsi/) says it is CC BY 4.0 for signals, transcription and some annotations. But that page says it was recorded on close-talking microphones. Another source says ICSI is a paid LDC corpus, and the [LDC catalogue entry](https://catalog.ldc.upenn.edu/LDC2004S02) lists the "LDC User Agreement for Non-Members" with the fee behind a login. It does have table-top mics, with about 72 hours across 75 meetings. If you want it, ask LDC about commercial terms. I couldn't see them, and you should confirm which distribution applies.
- **Fisher English:** It's paid LDC data, but it's telephone speech, not meetings or far-field.
- **AliMeeting and AISHELL-4:** These are far-field meeting corpora, but they're Mandarin.

## What I couldn't find
I found no commercially licensed English corpus that has real business meetings, far-field arrays and diarization labels beyond AMI. The paid route would be to ask a data vendor for custom-recorded meetings. I haven't researched specific vendors.

## Suggested next steps
1. Download AMI with the array audio and the manual annotations. Check the licence on the specific annotation files you use.
2. Add DiPCo for extra far-field data.
3. Ask LDC about commercial terms for ICSI, and a lawyer about CHiME-6's ShareAlike clause.
4. Evaluate on AMI. It's the standard benchmark, but your own recordings will tell you more about real-world performance.

Sources:
- [AMI licence](https://groups.inf.ed.ac.uk/ami/corpus/license.shtml)

- [ICSI at LDC](https://catalog.ldc.upenn.edu/LDC2004S02)

- [DiPCo on Zenodo](https://zenodo.org/records/8122551)
- [DiariZen licence issue](https://github.com/BUTSpeechFIT/DiariZen/issues/32)

Evidence (what the judge was shown; for an image, a description of what was sent)
**Recommendation: use AMI as your core dataset. Add DiPCo and CHiME-6 only as secondary sets for far-field robustness. There's no other free English meeting corpus that fits all your criteria.**

## 1. AMI Meeting Corpus (primary)
- **What it is:** About 100 hours of real, non-simulated meetings in English. Roughly two-thirds are scenario-driven, where participants play assigned roles, so they're staged but spoken naturally. The rest are natural meetings. It's the closest match to business-style meetings I found.
- **Audio:** Individual headsets, lapel mics, and a headset mix. The far-field audio comes from two table-top microphone arrays. The official download page lists it as "audio channels from two table-top arrays".
- **Licence:** The [AMI licence page](https://groups.inf.ed.ac.uk/ami/corpus/license.shtml) states that the corpus and its annotations are CC BY 4.0. That licence allows commercial use if you give attribution. The [download page](https://groups.inf.ed.ac.uk/ami/download/) says the manual (v1.6.2) and automatic (v1.5.1) annotation zips were also changed to CC BY 4.0. It adds that some other annotations may not be covered, so check the files you actually use.
- **Access:** Free download from the [AMI download page](https://groups.inf.ed.ac.uk/ami/download/). You pick meetings and audio streams there, and the annotations come as NXT-format zips. I didn't confirm which annotation file carries the speaker segmentation. The [annotation docs](https://groups.inf.ed.ac.uk/ami/corpus/annotation.shtml) should say.
- **Caveats:**
  - A Hugging Face card for `knkarthick/AMI` says "non-commercial". That contradicts the official CC BY 4.0 licence and looks like an error. Rely on the Edinburgh pages and keep a copy of the licence text.
  - Most speakers are non-native English speakers. The recordings are also from 2000s-era rooms, so they're a limited sample of modern conference-call audio.
  - Licences on pretrained models still matter. A pyannote or DiariZen checkpoint trained on mixed data can carry restrictions even though AMI itself is clean.

## 2. DiPCo (secondary, far-field)
- **What it is:** Dinner-party conversations, not meetings. It has 10 sessions of 15–45 minutes, with four people per session. Each person wore a close-talk mic. Five far-field devices with 7-mic arrays were placed around the room.
- **Licence:** CDLA-Permissive 1.0, which allows commercial use. The [Zenodo record](https://zenodo.org/records/8122551), the Interspeech paper and Amazon's release blog all agree.
- **Access:** Free from Zenodo (about 12 GB). The original S3 link has expired.
- **Caveat:** It's small, and the content is casual dinner talk.

## 3. CHiME-6 (secondary, far-field)
- **What it is:** English dinner-party recordings. It has 4 participants per session, recorded on several distant 4-mic Kinect arrays.
- **Licence:** CC BY-SA 4.0, listed on [OpenSLR SLR150](https://www.openslr.org/150/). That allows commercial use, but ShareAlike applies to derivatives. Have a lawyer decide whether your trained models count as derivatives before you use it for a commercial product.
- **Access:** Free from OpenSLR. Training data is about 97 GB, and the JSON transcriptions are a separate file.
- **Caveat:** Its content is domestic and very hard acoustically. It's useful for robustness, but it isn't meeting-like.

## Ruled out or not usable as-is
- **ICSI Meeting Corpus:** The Edinburgh [ICSI page](https://groups.inf.ed.ac.uk/ami/icsi/) says it is CC BY 4.0 for signals, transcription and some annotations. But that page says it was recorded on close-talking microphones. Another source says ICSI is a paid LDC corpus, and the [LDC catalogue entry](https://catalog.ldc.upenn.edu/LDC2004S02) lists the "LDC User Agreement for Non-Members" with the fee behind a login. It does have table-top mics, with about 72 hours across 75 meetings. If you want it, ask LDC about commercial terms. I couldn't see them, and you should confirm which distribution applies.
- **Fisher English:** It's paid LDC data, but it's telephone speech, not meetings or far-field.
- **AliMeeting and AISHELL-4:** These are far-field meeting corpora, but they're Mandarin.

## What I couldn't find
I found no commercially licensed English corpus that has real business meetings, far-field arrays and diarization labels beyond AMI. The paid route would be to ask a data vendor for custom-recorded meetings. I haven't researched specific vendors.

## Suggested next steps
1. Download AMI with the array audio and the manual annotations. Check the licence on the specific annotation files you use.
2. Add DiPCo for extra far-field data.
3. Ask LDC about commercial terms for ICSI, and a lawyer about CHiME-6's ShareAlike clause.
4. Evaluate on AMI. It's the standard benchmark, but your own recordings will tell you more about real-world performance.

Sources:
- [AMI licence](https://groups.inf.ed.ac.uk/ami/corpus/license.shtml)
- [AMI download](https://groups.inf.ed.ac.uk/ami/download/)
- [AMI overview](https://groups.inf.ed.ac.uk/ami/corpus/overview.shtml)
- [ICSI at Edinburgh](https://groups.inf.ed.ac.uk/ami/icsi/)
- [ICSI at LDC](https://catalog.ldc.upenn.edu/LDC2004S02)
- [CHiME-6 on OpenSLR](https://www.openslr.org/150/)
- [DiPCo on Zenodo](https://zenodo.org/records/8122551)
- [DiariZen licence issue](https://github.com/BUTSpeechFIT/DiariZen/issues/32)

- **Audio:** Individual headsets, lapel mics, and a headset mix. The far-field audio comes from two table-top microphone arrays. The official download page lists it as "audio channels from two table-top arrays".
- **Licence:** The [AMI licence page](https://groups.inf.ed.ac.uk/ami/corpus/license.shtml) states that the corpus and its annotations are CC BY 4.0. That licence allows commercial use if you give attribution. The [download page](https://groups.inf.ed.ac.uk/ami/download/) says the manual (v1.6.2) and automatic (v1.5.1) annotation zips were also changed to CC BY 4.0. It adds that some other annotations may not be covered, so check the files you actually use.
- **Access:** Free download from the [AMI download page](https://groups.inf.ed.ac.uk/ami/download/). You pick meetings and audio streams there, and the annotations come as NXT-format zips. I didn't confirm which annotation file carries the speaker segmentation. The [annotation docs](https://groups.inf.ed.ac.uk/ami/corpus/annotation.shtml) should say.
- **Caveats:**
  - A Hugging Face card for `knkarthick/AMI` says "non-commercial". That contradicts the official CC BY 4.0 licence and looks like an error. Rely on the Edinburgh pages and keep a copy of the licence text.
  - Most speakers are non-native English speakers. The recordings are also from 2000s-era rooms, so they're a limited sample of modern conference-call audio.
  - Licences on pretrained models still matter. A pyannote or DiariZen checkpoint trained on mixed data can carry restrictions even though AMI itself is clean.

## 2. DiPCo (secondary, far-field)
- **What it is:** Dinner-party conversations, not meetings. It has 10 sessions of 15–45 minutes, with four people per session. Each person wore a close-talk mic. Five far-field devices with 7-mic arrays were placed around the room.
- **Licence:** CDLA-Permissive 1.0, which allows commercial use. The [Zenodo record](https://zenodo.org/records/8122551), the Interspeech paper and Amazon's release blog all agree.
- **Access:** Free from Zenodo (about 12 GB). The original S3 link has expired.
- **Caveat:** It's small, and the content is casual dinner talk.

## 3. CHiME-6 (secondary, far-field)
- **What it is:** English dinner-party recordings. It has 4 participants per session, recorded on several distant 4-mic Kinect arrays.
- **Licence:** CC BY-SA 4.0, listed on [OpenSLR SLR150](https://www.openslr.org/150/). That allows commercial use, but ShareAlike applies to derivatives. Have a lawyer decide whether your trained models count as derivatives before you use it for a commercial product.
- **Access:** Free from OpenSLR. Training data is about 97 GB, and the JSON transcriptions are a separate file.
- **Caveat:** Its content is domestic and very hard acoustically. It's useful for robustness, but it isn't meeting-like.

## Ruled out or not usable as-is
- **ICSI Meeting Corpus:** The Edinburgh [ICSI page](https://groups.inf.ed.ac.uk/ami/icsi/) says it is CC BY 4.0 for signals, transcription and some annotations. But that page says it was recorded on close-talking microphones. Another source says ICSI is a paid LDC corpus, and the [LDC catalogue entry](https://catalog.ldc.upenn.edu/LDC2004S02) lists the "LDC User Agreement for Non-Members" with the fee behind a login. It does have table-top mics, with about 72 hours across 75 meetings. If you want it, ask LDC about commercial terms. I couldn't see them, and you should confirm which distribution applies.
- **Fisher English:** It's paid LDC data, but it's telephone speech, not meetings or far-field.
- **AliMeeting and AISHELL-4:** These are far-field meeting corpora, but they're Mandarin.

## What I couldn't find
I found no commercially licensed English corpus that has real business meetings, far-field arrays and diarization labels beyond AMI. The paid route would be to ask a data vendor for custom-recorded meetings. I haven't researched specific vendors.

## Suggested next steps
1. Download AMI with the array audio and the manual annotations. Check the licence on the specific annotation files you use.
2. Add DiPCo for extra far-field data.
3. Ask LDC about commercial terms for ICSI, and a lawyer about CHiME-6's ShareAlike clause.
4. Evaluate on AMI. It's the standard benchmark, but your own recordings will tell you more about real-world performance.

**Short answer: use the AMI Meeting Corpus.** It is the only dataset I found that meets all your requirements. Add ICSI as a smaller secondary option if you want more data.

## 1. AMI Meeting Corpus (recommended)

- **What it is:** About 100 hours of real English meetings with 3–5 participants. Many are scenario-driven design-team meetings, which means participants were role-playing a scenario. The rest are naturally occurring meetings. Most speakers are non-native.
- **Audio:** Individual headsets, a headset mix, and far-field audio from table-top microphone arrays. (The AMI download page lists the array audio as coming from two table-top arrays.)
- **Annotations:** Manual annotations are NXT XML, which includes word- and segment-level speaker timing. The download page doesn't mention RTTM files, so you would derive turn boundaries yourself.
- **Licence:** The Edinburgh licence page says "the AMI corpus and its annotations are released under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 license". CC BY 4.0 allows commercial use with attribution. The download page is narrower. It says the signals, the transcription and *some* annotations are CC BY 4.0, and it gives no licence for the DOME and social-role annotation sets. I did not find a list of exactly which annotations are covered. The manual and automatic annotation zips are stated to be CC BY 4.0.
- **Access:** Free download from the [AMI download page](https://groups.inf.ed.ac.uk/ami/download/). You select meetings and audio streams there, then unzip the annotation archives next to the signals.
- **Easier route for diarization:** [diarizers-community/ami on Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/datasets/diarizers-community/ami) is listed as CC-BY-4.0. It is about 21 GB of Parquet, with `timestamps_start`, `timestamps_end` and `speakers` fields. It loads with `load_dataset("diarizers-community/ami", "ihm")`. The page doesn't define the "ihm" and "sdm" subsets. I'd expect "ihm" to be headset and "sdm" to be a single distant microphone, but that is my assumption. For multichannel array audio, use the original download.

The upstream licence is clear, but I'd still keep a copy of the licence pages and the date you downloaded. Also check the Hugging Face copy against the original before you rely on it.

## 2. ICSI Meeting Corpus (secondary)

- **What it is:** About 70 hours of real research-group meetings. The recordings are close-talking microphones, available as separate SPH files or one mixed WAV. The Edinburgh page doesn't mention table-top microphones, so don't count on far-field audio from it.
- **Licence:** The [Edinburgh ICSI page](https://groups.inf.ed.ac.uk/ami/icsi/) says signals, transcription and some annotations are CC BY 4.0.
- **Caveat:** The same corpus is also sold through the LDC under terms that bar non-member for-profit organisations from commercial development. Use the Edinburgh copy, not the LDC one.

## What I ruled out

- **NOTSOFAR-1:** Real far-field array recordings, but a secondary source says it is CC BY-NC-ND. I did not check this myself, and I would confirm it before you spend time on it. If it is correct, it fails your commercial-use requirement.
- **LibriCSS:** The audio is played back through loudspeakers, not recorded in real meetings, so it doesn't fit.
- **CHiME-6:** English dinner-party conversations, not business meetings. I couldn't confirm its licence, so I wouldn't use it.
- **AliMeeting and LOTUSDIS:** Mandarin and Thai respectively, so they fail the English-only requirement.

## Mistakes in what I found

- One search result suggested that OpenSLR 106 was a CC-BY copy of ICSI. I checked, and it is a West African speech corpus under CC BY-SA 4.0. It has nothing to do with ICSI.
- A Hugging Face card (knkarthick/AMI) labels AMI "non-commercial licence: cc-by-4.0". That is self-contradictory and conflicts with Edinburgh's own terms. It looks like a third-party mislabel.

## Caveats

- **Domain gap:** AMI is a modest amount of data, with mostly scripted scenarios and one room set-up per site. For a commercial product, expect to need more in-domain data, and AMI will probably work better for evaluation than for training alone.
- **Paid options:** I did not find a commercially licensable real-meeting English corpus with array audio beyond AMI. You could commission recordings or negotiate with a data vendor. I haven't researched specific vendors.
- **Pretrained models:** If you fine-tune or ship pretrained diarization models, check their training-data licences too. A DiariZen maintainer noted that a checkpoint inherited non-commercial restrictions from other datasets in its training mix.

Sources:
- [AMI download page](https://groups.inf.ed.ac.uk/ami/download/)
- [AMI licence page](https://groups.inf.ed.ac.uk/ami/corpus/license.shtml)
- [AMI corpus page](https://groups.inf.ed.ac.uk/ami/corpus/)
- [ICSI at Edinburgh](https://groups.inf.ed.ac.uk/ami/icsi/)
- [diarizers-community/ami](https://huggingface.co/datasets/diarizers-community/ami)
- [OpenSLR 106](https://www.openslr.org/106/)
- [LDC licensing](https://www.ldc.upenn.edu/data-management/using/licensing)
- [DiariZen licence issue](https://github.com/BUTSpeechFIT/DiariZen/issues/32)
- [Meeting speech datasets comparison (Spirelight)](https://www.spirelight.ai/guides/meeting-speech-datasets)
